articles.title: Arch Manning leads Texas back from 20 points down in fourth quarter to shock No 1 Ohio State
articles.summary: Ohio State Buckeyes 23-24 Texas Longhorns Longhorns QB shows maturity in huge comeback Arch Manning delivered a moment, and it was a big one for Texas and himself. The Longhorns quarterback led No 4 Texas back from a 20-point fourth-quarter deficit to beat No 1 Ohio State 24-23 on Saturday night. Using his legs to keep drives going and his right arm to start the rally with a touchdown pass to Ryan Wingo, Manning delivered the kind of primetime performance that could redefine his career and propel the program’s national championship hopes. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Arch Manning delivered a moment, and it was a big one for Texas and himself. The Longhorns quarterback led No 4 Texas back from a 20-point fourth-quarter deficit to beat No 1 Ohio State 24-23 on Saturday night.

Using his legs to keep drives going and his right arm to start the rally with a touchdown pass to Ryan Wingo, Manning delivered the kind of primetime performance that could redefine his career and propel the program’s national championship hopes.

Grit that earned a piece of history. The Longhorns’ 20-point comeback in the fourth quarter is the largest fourth-quarter rally to win against an AP No 1 team, according to Sportradar.

Grit born out of the adversity of last season’s failures. Texas started last season No 1, lost at Ohio State and were soon unranked after a 3-2 start. Manning was the lightning rod for criticism because of erratic play in his first season as the full-time starter.

“Last September was a hard month for him,” Sarkisian said. “I think him getting through the adversity of last year helped him get through the adversity of tonight. When he comes back, everybody else comes back. That’s a guy who has some grit, some resilience.”

Saturday night initially looked like last season’s version of Manning and the Longhorns. His first pass was a completion that was fumbled away. Four plays later, a long throw turned into a fluke interception that set up Ohio State’s first touchdown and a 10-0 Buckeyes lead.

Nothing was working until Texas were backed up near their own end zone in the third quarter and losing 23-3. Manning took a big hit on the sideline as he made a desperate scramble. The hit seemed to wake up the entire offense. He completed 11 of his final 15 passes, directing three scoring drives of 12 plays or longer. Hollywood Smothers finished two of them with short touchdown runs, the last one with just 25 seconds left.

“It was a weird start,” Manning said. “I’m really proud of the way we responded. We could have let that thing go. It’s a testament to our coaches and our culture.”

Manning’s final stat line of 23-of-37 passing for 196 yards and a touchdown won’t light up a Heisman Trophy ballot. But pulling out the win in a game between two national championship contenders shows how far Manning has come as a competitor.

“We just had to get something going. I always knew we were going to be in it in the end,” Manning said. “I’m so glad we won.”

articles.title: Manchester United v Chelsea: Women’s Super League – live
articles.summary: ⚽️ WSL updates from 12pm BST at Leigh Sports Village ⚽️ Live scoreboard | Send your thoughts to Emillia via email The teams are out. Kick-off is just a few moments away! Ahead of today’s match, Chelsea head coach Sonia Bompastor said: “We need to keep the confidence and keep working hard. I spoke after the Villa game about the mentality, the mindset. It’s a huge part of being ruthless in the box. That game could have been easily 3-0 half-time, and we need to have that mentality when we have the opportunities to kill the game after 45 minutes to do that. Continue reading...
articles.content:
35 min: It’s all Chelsea now. United are struggling to get out of their own half.

A cross is sent into the box and Medina attempts to head it clear, but the ball only runs as far as Bronze, who shifts it to Walsh on her left. The midfielder sets herself up before unleashing a brilliant effort into the bottom-left corner.

Walsh makes it two for the girls in Blue! A great strike from the edge of the box.

29 min: Thompson plays a brilliant one-two with James on the left before running on the overlap and crossing the ball into the danger zone. Kaptein is there, but Miyazawa gets in front to head it away.

26 min: United break forward again as Park skips past McCabe before looking for the cross, but Buchanan makes the block to send the ball out for a corner.

24 min: Manchester United look to find a quick equaliser straight from kick-off as the ball is played through to Jusu Bah, who looks to break into the box but is flagged offside.

23 min: Chelsea unpick the Manchester United defence as Bronze sends a lofted pass into the box. Janssen completely mis-times the header, allowing Kaptein to take possession before squaring the ball across to Nüsken, who taps it in from close range.

19 min: Chelsea make their way into the box once again, but they almost try to walk the ball into the net! At least four players in Blue find themselves in a position to shoot but play it elsewhere. That might feel like an opportunity missed.

16 min: James puts the ball on a plate for Kaptein with a perfect cross from the left. The midfielder heads it towards goal, but there’s not enough conviction on it and Tullis-Joyce makes the save.

14 min: James receives the ball on the left side of the box after making a run over from the right. She cuts inside onto her right foot and unleashes a strike from the edge of the box, but it floats over the crossbar.

10 min: Chance for United as Terland receives the ball in a tight space in the box. She goes for goal but her effort is too weak and Hampton collects.

9 min: Chelsea seem to be operating in a 3-5-2 formation, with Nüsken and James the two leading the line. Bronze, Buchanan and McCabe are the back three.

6 min: The ball is brilliantly switched over to Jusu Bah on the left, who looks to make a run into the box, but Hampton rushes off her line to collect.

4 min: Bronze wins the ball back for Chelsea on the right side with a perfectly-timed challenge on Medina, who appeals for a free kick. Absolutely nothing wrong with that tackle. Play continues.

2 min: Chelsea attempt to cause some early problems for United as the ball is sent into James, who taps it just wide.

Ahead of today’s match, Chelsea head coach Sonia Bompastor said: “We need to keep the confidence and keep working hard. I spoke after the Villa game about the mentality, the mindset. It’s a huge part of being ruthless in the box. That game could have been easily 3-0 half-time, and we need to have that mentality when we have the opportunities to kill the game after 45 minutes to do that.

“This week I was coaching the players in the final details: around timings of the runs in the box, being in the right zones, what type of crosses do we want to deliver, what are the connections between the crosser and the players who are making the runs in the box.

“It’s just for me to reinforce those messages, to coach them on the pitch, and make sure we get them right on the game on the weekend.”

“Don’t panic; that has to be United’s message. To an extent, it is very early to be writing the team’s obituary. The new head coach, Eva Olid, had only three weeks to try to implement her ideas about the way the team should play before that match against London City Lionesses on Friday 4 September. That is not long enough for her to peel away Marc Skinner’s imprint on the team…”

In her pre-match press conference, Manchester United head coach Eva Olid said: “I expect us to be confident with the ball, everyone showing we want to have the ball. It’s everything like that, not just about confidence.

“Of course we know they are good and there will be moments we have to defend, but we want to attack too, we want to put them in difficult situations where we hurt them, and that is the main focus.

“When we have the ball, we enjoy the ball, and we really have confidence to create chances, put them in difficult situations and hope that we can score goals too.”

In case you missed it, London City Lionesses suffered a 2-1 defeat to West Ham yesterday. Kelly Gago and Viviane Asseyi were on target for the Hammers at the Chigwell Construction Stadium.

Melvine Malard is not available to face her former club today after suffering a knock in training. The Blues are also without Mayra Ramirez and Manaka Matsukubo.

Meanwhile, Jayde Riviere and Emma Watson are absent from the Manchester United squad.

Manchester United starting XI: Phallon Tullis-Joyce; Hanna Lundkvist, Maya Le Tissier (C), Dominique Janssen, Andrea Medina; Hinata Miyazawa, Julia Zigiotti; Jess Park, Ella Toone, Monica Jusu Bah; Elisabeth Terland.

Subs: Janina Leitzig, Scarlett Hill, Anna Sandberg, Jess Simpson, Jess Anderson, Simi Awujo, Rebeca Bernal, Mared Griffiths, Lea Schüller.

Chelsea starting line-up: Hannah Hampton; Ellie Carpenter, Lucy Bronze (C), Kadeisha Buchanan, Katie McCabe; Keira Walsh, Lexi Potter; Sjoeke Nüsken, Wieke Kaptein, Alyssa Thompson; Lauren James.

Subs: Livia Peng, Veerle Buurman, Nathalie Björn, Giulia Dragoni, Nelly Las, Maika Hamano, Sandy Baltimore, Aggie Beever-Jones.

Hello and welcome to coverage of the WSL meeting between Manchester United and Chelsea. Both teams dropped points in their opening games last weekend, with United suffering a 2-1 loss to London City Lionesses and Chelsea held to a 1-1 draw by Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge.

Today presents a completely different challenge. The Blues have won five of their last six games against United, with the remaining fixture resulting in a draw.

However, given it’s just the start of a new campaign, anything can happen.

articles.title: Rangers v Celtic: Scottish League Cup quarter-final – live
articles.summary: Match at Ibrox kicks off at 12pm (all times BST) Miovski hits late Rangers winner, Celtic extend streak 7 min: Celtic are looking just a touch sloppy here, with Rangers setting the rhythm as Penrice wins the ball in midfield. 5 min: A shocker at the back from Johnstone, clearing the ball straight to Kelsy, inside the area, who hooks it wide. Celtic get away with one early. Continue reading...
articles.content:
34 min: Makhanya continues to impress on the ball, keeping Rangers ticking … Gassama overdoes it on the left, dribbling out of play when he had the chance to cut back.

31 min: Celtic do have space to exploit on the counter, but they’ve failed to properly test Pandur.

28 min: Min-su and Penrice are over the ball … the latter crosses and Fernandez leaps … but he can’t keep his header down.

27 min: Gassama is causing problems down the left, beating Donovan, who takes him down. Free-kick to Rangers and another yellow for Celtic.

25 min: Durán finds a bit of space by the edge of the area for a shot … but it’s straight at Pandur.

Naderi finds the ball in the left channel, hooks it to Kelsy inside the area, and he finds Neil inside the D with plenty of space. The midfielder is calm amid the madness, locating the bottom left corner. Derek McInnes is a happy, happy man. That goal has been coming.

22 min: It’s a poor delivery for the free-kick and Celtic counter … but Makhanya, who has been very composed, continues to clear up at the back.

21 min: Gassama twists and turns on the left for Rangers , sending in a dangerous low ball into the area … it’s cleared away but Rangers have a free-kick from the right.

19 min: The energy has picked up in the last few minutes as Celtic advance … but here comes a yellow card for Nygren, who slides in on Kelsy.

15 min: Huge chance. Penrice whips in a delicious cross form the left and Johnstone flaps at the ball … it drops for Min-su inside the area, he connects well, but Scales gets a vital touch to deny Rangers the opener. Celtic’s keeper has made an iffy start here.

13 min: Time for Rangers to go long with a throw, Sterling to send it in from the right … the ball works it way back to Sterling, whose low cross is blocked for a corner.

11 min: Celtic push down the left-hand side, with Tierney ready for a long throw … but Fernandez heads away. Rangers counter but Donovan wins it back for Celtic, the move closing with Durán dragging a tame shot wide.

9 min: Durán tries to drive down the right for Celtic , but Makhanya gets in the way.

7 min: Celtic are looking just a touch sloppy here, with Rangers setting the rhythm as Penrice wins the ball in midfield.

5 min: A shocker at the back from Johnstone, clearing the ball straight to Kelsy, inside the area, who hooks it wide. Celtic get away with one early.

3 min: Makhanya rushes forward and takes down Durán inside Celtic’s half.

2 min: Rangers build and Gassama collects on the left, cuts inside … but the shot lacks venom, cleaned up comfortably by Johnstone in the Celtic net.

1 min: Rangers knock it around at the back before Makhanya goes long, down the left-hand side.

Sam Johnstone, who has joined Celtic on loan from Wolves, made his debut in the league this week and keeps his place. The Hoops have made four changes from midweek, with Kieran Tierney, Cameron Carter-Vickers, Benjamin Nygren and Camilo Durán all starting today. Haissem Hassan, my World Cup hero , must settle for a spot on the bench.

There won’t be any Celtic support at Ibrox today – the SPFL announced this month that away fans will not attend Old Firm derbies in its competitions this season. There was fan disorder when the two sides met in March in the Scottish Cup.

Rangers: Pandur, Sterling, Fernandez, Makhanya, Penrice, Neil, Raskin, Min-su, Gassama, Kelsy, Naderi

Subs: Kelly, McCrorie, Godfrey, Dragojevic, Devlin, Chukwuani, Curtis, Bouanani, Miovski

Celtic: Johnstone, Donovan, Carter-Vickers, Scales, Tierney, McGregor, Baur, Nygren, Durán, Tounekti, Høgh

Subs: Sinisalo, Lotomba, Trusty, Sørensen, Oxlade-Chamberlain, Hassan, Mheuka, Murray, Forrest

Hello, hello, hello and welcome to the first Old Firm derby of the season. Forget the league, where Celtic have a 100% record, and forget Europe, where there’s been serious misery for both sides . We go to the League Cup, won by St Mirren last time round, Wilfried Nancy’s side beaten in the final . He was gone not long after, prompting the return of Martin O’Neill.

This’ll be the first time Derek McInnes comes up against Celtic as Rangers’ manager, with his side having won four on the bounce after a difficult start. It’ll also be McInnes’ first meeting with Celtic since that day in May , when his Hearts side couldn’t hold on to claim the title. We won’t have that level of drama today … but it should still be fun. Kick-off’s at 12pm BST.

However she repeats the error of the 1st hole, leaving a dribbler short, failing to take into account the slowness of the wet greens. A let-off for Hull. 1UP Hull v Khang (2) Henseleit A/S Al. Lee (1) Grant v Yin Continue reading...
articles.content:
Auston Kim misses a short birdie putt on 4, and Lottie Woad, who had already converted, hits the front. Megan Khang shaves the cup on 11; so close to a bounceback birdie, but Charley Hull remains 2UP. And Celine Boutier leaves a birdie putt one roll short on 1, so no fast start for Europe in the anchor match. But Mimi Rhodes rattles in a 15-footer for birdie at 8 to halve the hole and hang on in there against Nelly Korda.

2UP Hull v Khang (11) 4UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (9) 3UP Grant v Yin (8) Rhodes v Korda 2UP (8) 2UP Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz (6) Nadaud A/S An. Lee (4) Lopez Ramirez A/S Noh (4) 1UP Woad v Kim (4) Maguire v Coughlin 1UP (3) Stark A/S Duncan (2) Ciganda A/S Kupcho (1) Boutier A/S Zhang (1)

Par is enough to win the 6th hole for Nanna Madsen. Europe looking good at the top end of the scoreboard, but with so many players currently on terms, you’d be a brave soul to bet the farm on the outcome.

2UP Hull v Khang (10) 4UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (9) 3UP Grant v Yin (8) Rhodes v Korda 2UP (7) 2UP Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz (6) Nadaud A/S An. Lee (4) Lopez Ramirez A/S Noh (4) Woad A/S Kim (3) Maguire v Coughlin 1UP (2) Stark A/S Duncan (2) Ciganda A/S Kupcho (1) Boutier v Zhang

A third birdie of the day for the world number one Nelly Korda, this time at 7. She moves a couple up against Mimi Rhodes. Linn Grant and Angel Yin both make their birdie putts on 8, the latter snapping that dismal five-bogey streak. Charley Hull’s two big hits into 10 prove enough to win the hole and double her lead over Megan Khang. Meanwhile Celine Boutier and Rose Zhang arrive on the 1st tee, and now all of the matches are out on the course.

Linn Grant cops a decent lie on a bald spot amid the heather down the right of 8. She takes advantage of her good fortune by wedging to eight feet. That turns the pressure up on Angel Yin, but she clips crisply out of the bunker to six feet. Putting contest coming up. Meanwhile Lottie Woad and Auston Kim trade birdies on 3, the former with an iron to four feet, the latter with a 20-foot putt. And on 4, Yealimi Noh and Julia Lopez Ramirez take turns to miss three-footers and the hole is somehow halved.

Angel Yin has made five bogeys in a row. But she’s got the advantage on the short par-four 8th, finding the bunker guarding the front left of the green, Linn Grant flaying her tee shot towards heather down the right. Meanwhile up on the par-five 10th, Charley Hull hammers a fairway wood onto the front of the green to set up a long eagle chance. Her opponent Megan Khang is forced to lay up.

Having found water on 5, Angel Yin does it again on 7. Her ball in a creek guarding the front of the green. It costs her another hole. Julia Lopez Ramirez birdies 3 to level against Yealimi Noh. Meanwhile Nelly Korda drains a 25-footer on 6 to regain the lead against Mimi Rhodes.

1UP Hull v Khang (9) 4UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (8) 3UP Grant v Yin (7) Rhodes v Korda 1UP (6) 1UP Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz (4) Nadaud A/S An. Lee (4) Lopez Ramirez A/S Noh (3) Woad A/S Kim (2) Maguire v Coughlin 1UP (1) Stark A/S Duncan (1) Ciganda v Kupcho

It’s going extremely well for Europe at the moment. Even a birdie for Yealimi Noh on 2, which gives her the lead against Julia Lopez Ramirez, doesn’t change that. But the USA have started slowly in most of the disciplines so far, and managed to fight their way back on the later holes. There’s a long way to go. It’s still absolutely hosing down, by the way.

Birdie for Mimi Rhodes at 5, and the rookie has tied up her match against the world number one Nelly Korda! Another European rookie, Nastasia Nadaud, levels up against Andrea Lee, the latter having found that water. And so for a few seconds, there’s no red on the board … until Lauren Coughlin walks in a par putt on 1 to go up early doors against Leona Maguire. Meanwhile Alison Lee’s antics down 7 hands another hole to Esther Henselit, as expected.

1UP Hull v Khang (8) 4UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (7) 2UP Grant v Yin (6) Rhodes A/S Korda (5) 1UP Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz (4) Nadaud A/S An. Lee (3) Lopez Ramirez A/S Noh (1) Woad A/S Kim (1) Maguire v Coughlin 1UP (1) Stark v Duncan

Angel Yin misses the green at the par-three 6th, and it’s another hole for Linn Grant. Her third in four holes. Yin’s lack of competitive action catching up with her big-time. Alison Lee sends her third at 3 into a greenside bunker. And a messy double bogey by Nanna Madsen on 4 cuts her lead in half.

Not a good moment if your name is Lee. Alison’s tee shot at 7 ends up under a tree atop some pine cones, and she’s forced to punch out. Esther Henseleit finds the green in regulation and the US are in a spot of bother there. See also Andrea on 3, as her ball takes a flyer, whistling through the green and towards the water behind. She might have gone through the reeds and in, it’s not clear from the pictures. Either way, it’s not going to be good news for her.

Esther Henseleit becomes the first player today to go three holes up. Her tee shot at the par-three 6th finds the meat of the green; Alison Lee’s effort bounds through and down the swale at the back. Lee can’t get up and down, and par is enough for the German. Angel Yin’s visit to the water on 5 costs her the hole and gifts Linn Grant the lead. But there’s better news for the USA on 2, where Andrea Lee’s birdie puts some red on the board.

1UP Hull v Khang (7) 3UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (6) 1UP Grant v Yin (5) Rhodes v Korda 1UP (4) 2UP Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz (3) Nadaud v An. Lee 1UP (2) Lopez Ramirez A/S Noh (1) Woad v Kim

Angel Yin started fast, but having not played so much golf this year, the rust is beginning to show. She carves her third at 5 into the drink on the right. As if it isn’t wet enough.

The rain is coming down in stair rods now. Players taking their shots as quickly as possible before scuttling back under the nearest umbrella. It’s cold as well. In theory, these conditions should favour the Europeans, who will be more used to them … but Angela Stanford sent her players out to practice under a deluge on Wednesday, and was at pains to emphasise that the US are prepared and ready to deal with wet weather. Thrills and spills ahoy!

Nanna Madsen looks to have benefitted from putting her feet up yesterday. She’s now followed birdie at 1 with another at 2, and she’s flown out of the traps. See also Esther Henseleit, who rolls in a 15-footer on 5 for birdie and Europe are 2UP in that match as well!

1UP Hull v Khang (6) 2UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (5) Grant A/S Yin (4) Rhodes v Korda 1UP (3) 2UP Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz (2) Nadaud A/S An. Lee (1) Lopez Ramirez v Noh

Nastasia Nadaud and Andrea Lee take turns to shave the lip with mid-range birdie putts on 1. Up on 4, Angel Yin leaves a monster birdie effort a good ten feet short, and doesn’t lose her turn. She can’t make the par saver … but Linn Grant spurns the opportunity to win the hole from five feet, her ball breaking away on the low side. Grant doesn’t concede Yin’s bogey putt, which to be fair looks well inside the leather. Gauntlet down, gloves off, Yin converts but doesn’t look particularly happy about it. That may have been the entire point, of course.

1UP Hull v Khang (5) 1UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (4) Grant A/S Yin (4) Rhodes v Korda 1UP (2) 1UP Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz (1) Nadaud A/S An. Lee (1) Lopez Ramirez v Noh

Charley Hull has a reasonably straight six-footer on 5 for birdie and the win. But she leaves it up on the high side. Bit of a misread. An opportunity goes by. The rain is getting heavier.

Mimi Rhodes isn’t close at 2. Nelly Korda is. Rhodes leaves a 50-foot putt ten short, but she doesn’t get the opportunity to make par, because Korda steers in a gentle left-to-right curler from eight feet to hit the front in that match. Meanwhile bogey for Angel Yin at 3 gifts Linn Grant parity in match three.

1UP Hull v Khang (4) 1UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (4) Grant A/S Yin (3) Rhodes v Korda 1UP (2) 1UP Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz (1) Nadaud v An. Lee

Allisen Corpuz – in the bunker at the back of 1, having earlier been forced to chop out from the heather – has to hole out for the half. She can’t do it. Europe go 1UP. Back on the tee, the latest match to go out is Andrea Lee versus the impressive rookie Nastasia Nadaud, the youngest player here this week. Two points in the bag for the 21-year-old French star-in-the-making already.

Charley Hull carves her tee shot at the par-three 4th into rough to the right of the green. But she nearly holes the chip up, and that’s enough to scramble the half and retain her lead. Meanwhile on 1, Allisen Corpuz becomes the latest US player to find the bunker at the back of the green. Nanna Madsen nearly does the same, but her ball grabs the last bit of green and spins back to 12 feet. Advantage Europe in that one.

Mimi Rhodes very nearly drains a 30-footer on 1 for an early lead. But the ball stops one turn short. Not many putts racing past the hole so far. Not any . Back on the tee, Allisen Corpuz pulls her opening drive into the heather down the left. Her ball rears up and hits a marshal on the jacksie, a lovely cartoon touch. But back into the heather it disappears. From bracket to bracken. Nanna Madsen, freshly rested after a day off, splits the fairway. Meanwhile up on 2, Angel Yin spins her approach to kick-in range, and that’s the first dash of red on the board this morning.

1UP Hull v Khang (3) 1UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (2) Grant v Yin 1UP (2) Rhodes A/S Korda (1) Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz

Alison Lee gets a bit of a flyer out of wet semi-rough down the right of 2. She doesn’t get close to the flag, and though she lags her long birdie putt up to tap-in distance, Esther Henseleit has thrown a dart to six feet from the centre of the fairway and tidies up for birdie. Another splash of blue on the scoreboard. That putt only just dropped, though. The greens slow, to belabour the point.

1UP Hull v Khang (3) 1UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (2) Grant A/S Yin (1) Rhodes v Korda

The greens haven’t run this slow all week: 10 on the stimp compared to 10.3 yesterday. And the players are struggling with the pace in these early matches. Angel Yin and Linn Grant become the latest to leave fairly straight birdie putts a couple of inches short on 1. Back on the tee, the world number one Nelly Korda prepares to face the rookie Mimi Rhodes, who already has two points in the bag for Europe this week. She’s on record as saying she loves a challenge and the heat of battle; she’s certainly got all of that on her plate today. They both find the wide, generous fairway.

1UP Hull v Khang (2) Henseleit A/S Al. Lee (1) Grant A/S Yin (1) Rhodes v Korda

Charley Hull lets go of her club – a wet grip? – while sending her second at the par-five 2nd into a fairway bunker. She whips into the green and makes par, but Megan Khang set up a six-foot birdie chance to level the match. However she repeats the error of the 1st hole, leaving a dribbler short, failing to take into account the slowness of the wet greens. A let-off for Hull.

Angel Yin hasn’t played too much golf recently – she’s been ill earlier in the year, and sat out yesterday altogether – but displays no nerves in sending her opening drive down the middle. Linn Grant follows her. Up on the green, Alison Lee gets up and down from the bunker to salvage a half.

With the rain still coming down, and forecast to get heavier in the early afternoon, it’s preferred lies today. Finding the fairway more important than ever. But you still have to take advantage. Esther Henseleit throws a dart at the flagstick on 1, her ball ten feet shy of the pin. But Alison Lee makes exactly the same mistake Megan Khang did, finding the bunker at the back. She’s left with a slight downhill lie and not much green to play with. More good news for Europe coming up?

The US captain Angela Stanford references Jennifer Kupcho’s heroics as she makes a bullish statement to Sky: “We needed a jolt … they’re all fired up this morning … I’m pretty confident in the end of our line-up … they’re ready.”

Esther Henseleit and Alison Lee take turns to split the fairway with their opening drives. Up on the green, Megan Khang doesn’t give her five-footer enough oomph, the moisture on the green doing a number on her. The ball stays on the edge. The door open for Hull, and she walks on through. First blood to Europe!

Hull is further from the flag so will take her putt first. A 30-footer with some right-to-left swing. She leaves the putt three feet short, the morning rain having slowed the greens. Khang splashes out from the bunker to five feet. A couple of little testers coming up. Back on the tee, the second match of Esther Henseleit and Alison Lee arrives for work. Bedlam, bedlam, bedlam.

The adrenaline must be pumping … and Megan Khang sends her approach through the green into a bunker at the back of 1. She can’t believe it. “Long?!” she asks her caddie. It’s long. Charley Hull responds with a slightly conservative play, finding the heart of the green, the pin tucked back left near Khang’s bunker. But that’s a slight advantage to Europe.

Europe captain Anna Nordqvist has a simple message for Sky Sports: “We’re on a mission today.”

Here we go, then … it’s come to this. A rainy day at Bernardus Golf in Cromvoirt near Den Bosch in North Brabant, Netherlands. The gallery in good voice nonetheless. The first match of Charley Hull and Megan Khang receive the ovation they deserve. Both players have led their team out before, Khang beating Linn Grant in 2023, Hull seeing off Nelly Korda in 2024. That experience sees them good as they both pump fine drives down the track. No going back now!

It was a classic matchplay double whammy. An all-timer. Yesterday evening in the gloaming , with Europe looking likely to take a 9-7 lead into the Sunday singles, Jennifer Kupcho tramlined a 90-footer on 17 before guiding in a 30-footer on the last to pull the rug spectacularly, skilfully, nervelessly, dramatically from under the feet of the astonished hosts and level the scores at 8-8. A genuine Where Were You When …? event, 120 feet’s worth of brilliance you’ll see again and again and again and again for ever more. And you can double that should the USA win and/or retain the trophy this afternoon! Take it to the bank. Jennifer Kupcho: instant Solheim Cup legend.

Can Europe recover from that late, late, great bodyblow? They’ve got 12 chances to do so. They need six-and-a-half more points to regain the Solheim Cup; the USA require a mere six to retain. If the first two days are anything to go by – and Carlota Ciganda’s Seve-and-Spieth-infused heroics on Friday now seem a sepia-tinged dot in the dim and distant past in this post-Kupcho multicoloured world – this is going to be very tense, very dramatic … and an awful lot of fun. It’s on!

With the rain still coming down, and forecast to get heavier in the early afternoon, it’s preferred lies today. Finding the fairway more important than ever. But you still have to take advantage. Esther Henseleit throws a dart at the flagstick on 1, her ball ten feet shy of the pin. But Alison Lee makes exactly the same mistake Megan Khang did, finding the bunker at the back. She’s left with a slight downhill lie and not much green to play with. More good news for Europe coming up?

The US captain Angela Stanford references Jennifer Kupcho’s heroics as she makes a bullish statement to Sky: “We needed a jolt … they’re all fired up this morning … I’m pretty confident in the end of our line-up … they’re ready.”

Esther Henseleit and Alison Lee take turns to split the fairway with their opening drives. Up on the green, Megan Khang doesn’t give her five-footer enough oomph, the moisture on the green doing a number on her. The ball stays on the edge. The door open for Hull, and she walks on through. First blood to Europe!

Hull is further from the flag so will take her putt first. A 30-footer with some right-to-left swing. She leaves the putt three feet short, the morning rain having slowed the greens. Khang splashes out from the bunker to five feet. A couple of little testers coming up. Back on the tee, the second match of Esther Henseleit and Alison Lee arrives for work. Bedlam, bedlam, bedlam.

The adrenaline must be pumping … and Megan Khang sends her approach through the green into a bunker at the back of 1. She can’t believe it. “Long?!” she asks her caddie. It’s long. Charley Hull responds with a slightly conservative play, finding the heart of the green, the pin tucked back left near Khang’s bunker. But that’s a slight advantage to Europe.
Europe captain Anna Nordqvist has a simple message for Sky Sports: “We’re on a mission today.”

Here we go, then … it’s come to this. A rainy day at Bernardus Golf in Cromvoirt near Den Bosch in North Brabant, Netherlands. The gallery in good voice nonetheless. The first match of Charley Hull and Megan Khang receive the ovation they deserve. Both players have led their team out before, Khang beating Linn Grant in 2023, Hull seeing off Nelly Korda in 2024. That experience sees them good as they both pump fine drives down the track. No going back now!

It was a classic matchplay double whammy. An all-timer. Yesterday evening in the gloaming , with Europe looking likely to take a 9-7 lead into the Sunday singles, Jennifer Kupcho tramlined a 90-footer on 17 before guiding in a 30-footer on the last to pull the rug spectacularly, skilfully, nervelessly, dramatically from under the feet of the astonished hosts and level the scores at 8-8. A genuine Where Were You When …? event, 120 feet’s worth of brilliance you’ll see again and again and again and again for ever more. And you can double that should the USA win and/or retain the trophy this afternoon! Take it to the bank. Jennifer Kupcho: instant Solheim Cup legend.

Can Europe recover from that late, late, great bodyblow? They’ve got 12 chances to do so. They need six-and-a-half more points to regain the Solheim Cup; the USA require a mere six to retain. If the first two days are anything to go by – and Carlota Ciganda’s Seve-and-Spieth-infused heroics on Friday now seem a sepia-tinged dot in the dim and distant past in this post-Kupcho multicoloured world – this is going to be very tense, very dramatic … and an awful lot of fun. It’s on!

articles.content:
That concludes the blog for today , with plenty of action to follow in the Premier League, and these two currently live.

Rangers lead Celtic 1-0 in the Scottish League Cup , while Chelsea lead at Manchester United in the WSL.

“Despite a good pre-season and positive signs, the team failed to achieve the desired results in the Bundesliga,” sporting director Rouven Schröder said. “Recent performances led to the decision to relieve Eugen of his duties with immediate effect. Eugen is a true ‘Borusse’ through and through.”

“It hurts so much that things have turned out this way,” said Polanski, the former Under-23 team coach. “After successfully securing our top-flight status (last season), we made a number of changes for this season. We had big ambitions but failed to put them into practice.”

Telling Opta stat here: “Morgan Gibbs-White has either scored or assisted in each of his last eight Premier League away games (6G, 4A); only Erling Haaland (September 2023), Robin van Persie (May 2011), and Andrew Cole (December 1993) have enjoyed longer runs in the competition (all 9).”

Since people sometimes like to share updates on other teams and leagues in these weekend posts, I'll give a summary of Denmark's Superliga, a league I know everybody here follows closely but would be interested in a write-up of anyway.

Sadly, it looks like business as usual is going to be restored at the top. FC København, having finished in the bottom half for the first time since the late 90s last season, are top and in outstanding form. Clear favorites for the title. The club with whom they have typically fought for the title over the past 12 years, FC Midtjylland, currently sit second.

If there are going to be any surprise challengers for the title, it looks like it will be the club in my name, FC Nordsjælland. FCN are a club who quite often have a decent-to-excellent attack, but are porous at the back. This season so far, they have the joint-fewest goals conceded and have looked quite solid defensively. It looks like their best chance in years to grab their second-ever title, though we'll see how they cope with only their third-ever European league/group stage.

Speaking of Europe, Denmark have for the first time since (I think) 2014 improved their coefficient to the point where this season they have two Champions League spots. Sadly, they have no teams in the Champions League or Europa League, but this might be a blessing in disguise, because they have a whole four teams in the Conference League, and they might be able to pick up enough coefficient points to improve their standing.

Last season's shock champions, AGF, are off to a shocking start, sitting second-bottom after seven games and not having yet won a game. After winning their first title in 40 years last season (think Hearts without the heartbreak at the end), nobody really expected them to repeat, but still...

The two promoted clubs, Lyngby and Horsens, are off to good starts. Lyngby are not surprising, they are quite the yo-yo club over the past decade, but spent three straight seasons in the Superliga before going down for a season to the second tier. Horsens' start are more impressive, given that it's their first in the top flight in 13 years.

Not many Mancunians in today’s Manchester derby but Kobbie Mainoo will be one of them.

There has been a spotlight on Mainoo, with some fans wondering how he would react to the suffocation of his World Cup dream; his treatment by Tuchel, who preferred Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice in the deeper midfield positions and, also, at various times, Reece James, Jude Bellingham, Jordan Henderson, Morgan Rogers and Nico O’Reilly. Nobody should have worried. Mainoo is made of stern stuff. United regeared their midfield to the tune of £155m during the transfer window, adding Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba. Baleba has not yet played because of injury, but as United prepare for Sunday’s derby at Old Trafford, it is Mainoo who has reasserted himself.

Fulham are among the Premier League’s winless wonders but Alvaro Arbeloa is not panicking, particularly not after that goalless draw at Liverpool.

“I know that when you are not winning games it’s not so easy that your players believe in your ideas. But they believe in the way that we have been working and I am so happy and so proud of the way that we played.

“I want that my players show this character, that they want the ball, they want the ball under pressure. We know what we have to do, how we could beat the pressure of Liverpool and we did so, so well against a team that press so high and so well.

I think there were so many things that we did well, but we have been making mistakes and of course in this league, if you make mistakes, they will punish you. If you have chances, try to take those chances but also to be a little bit more balanced. I think we did better and we realised how important it is to be balanced.”

Nottingham Forest defender Nikola Milenkovic is set for three weeks on the sidelines with a hamstring injury.

The Serbia international suffered the problem on the eve of Saturday’s 2-1 win at Aston Villa and is definitely out of next week’s clash with Coventry. “Nikola is a little bit more serious,” boss Oliver Glasner said. “He will also miss Coventry. We are hopeful that he can be back after the international break. Let’s say this is the first time I feel three weeks without a game is good.” (Press Association)

Another fun fact: “West Ham have been relegated and played seven Championship games but still scored a Premier League goal more recently than Tottenham Hotspur.”

Bournemouth really will do well with the amount of chances they are creating. If they can be clinical they will be a dangerous team. Raya is a wonderful goal keeper. The Sunderland vs Arsenal game was a but of a grim watch. Hull deserved their point against Chelsea. Martinez is making Sanchez look solid in the Chelsea goal. That Chelsea defence...dearie me. Villa's defence is also all over the place. Delap sparks to life. Liverpool are wide open at the back - creating (and not converting) from the front. Fulham are the fun team this season with loads of endeavour but not the results.

My Spurs still goalless. Another grim watch. Whilst we can commend the fact that the defence and midfield is looking better - it's right to be asking much more from Spurs forward players. It's OK to criticise Tel for his decision making - but by that same reasoning what excuse do Marmoush, Solanke and Savio have? Solanke remains a ghost of the player he was. He drifted through this game with zero impact.

Again this highlights the Richarlison folly. Spurs top PL scorer from last season of the players that started against Everton was Van de Ven with 4. No player in the Spurs starting 11 scored more than 4 goals last season. Palhinha and Romero have moved on. If Richarlison said he wanted to leave at the beginning of the summer why did they wait till the end of the transfer window to sell him? Fishy. Richarlison 15 goal involvements last season watching from the stands - illegible to play. Make it make sense. Spurs needed an out and out striker this summer.

To put Spurs goalscoring woes into perspective. If Coventry and Hamburg score today - Spurs will be the only team in Europe's top five leagues not to score a goal. That includes the whole English football divisions.

Patience of course - and small improvements each game - Van Hecke and Tonali really settling in. But goals decide if a season will be a struggle or fruitful.

Rangers: Pandur, Sterling, Fernandez, Makhanya, Penrice, Neil, Raskin, Minsu, Gassama, Kelsy, Naderi. Subs: Kelly, McCrorie, Godfrey, Dragojecic, Devlin, Chukwuani, Curtis, Bouanani, Movski

Celtic: Johnstone, Donovan, Carter-Vickers, Scales, Tierney, Baur, McGregor, Nygren, Duran, Hogh, Tounekti. Subs: Sinisalo, Lotomba, Trusty, Sorensen, Oxlade-Chamberlain, Mheuka, Hassan, Forrest, Murray

Another stat from that Liverpool draw with Fulham, via the BBC : “Isak’s 16 touches in 90 minutes was the second fewest for an outfield Reds player on record, having had the fewest (14) against Forest a fortnight ago.”

This isn’t the Isak we saw at Newcastle, is it? Odd for an Iraola team. At Bournemouth, Evanilson was always involved.

Bundesliga news: Borussia Mönchengladbach have dismissed Eugen Polanski with immediate effect, after their 5-0 loss to Freiburg. Just three games in, too.

More De Zerbi, on his post-match discussion with Mathys Tel: “Yes, I coached him on the pitch. The body shape. He is a striker and the striker can play with the shoulder on the goal.

“If we are playing with Maddison, Kudus and Savio, [Tel] has to play as a striker and the striker has to look at the goal or the cross from Robertson. He has to stay inside because he started as a striker eh? Now he is playing as a winger but he started his career as a striker, but I love Mathys as a player, as a guy and there is not a problem.”

Here’s a decent stat, via Fulham: “Álvaro Arbeloa is the first manager to take points from Liverpool having also played for them in the Premier League.”

Who would that take in? Steven Gerrard? Xabi Alonso yet to face them? Why have so few ex-Liverpool players managed the Premier League? Gary McAllister? ⚪️

And with that, John Brewin is here to continue the build-up to this afternoon’s games.

Got a minute to spare? Why not try our daily Premier League trivia game, On the ball? Every day a star player past or present is hidden behind nine clues. How many will you need to identify them?

The Guardian's daily football game , On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?

Jamie Jackson has previewed today’s Manchester derby. You can give it a read below…

Now, let’s look ahead to the Manchester derby. Is there a clear favourite for this one? I’m not sure there is. I suppose most people would expect City to win, but United pulled off a shock result in this fixture last season.

In case you missed Mauricio Pochettino’s comments this week, the former Tottenham boss argued that Spurs should be awarded Chelsea’s 2016-17 Premier League title.

He said: “We should win one Premier League, we should have been awarded it. If that [Chelsea’s rule-break] was true, then we deserve to be champions that year, for sure. They were punished, they admitted it? So that’s it. The title should be for the team that was second.

“We can say that they scored goals, they won games. OK. But it’s completely fair to say that we didn’t compete before the start of the season with the same card. Maybe with the same rules, we could’ve signed some players that would have made the team better or scored more goals.”

Dave Estherby has messaged in about Tottenham and their (lack of) goalscoring. He says:

“Re. question of the day (8.44), yes, they will score (a) goal(s) - they will also finally achieve their, er, goal of getting relegated at the third time of asking. New manager, fortune spent, zero difference. Conte and Ange were right, it’s a business not a football club. As long as they can fill that stadium with Jay Z/Jacksonville Jaguars fans all is well.

“The fact Pochettino is now trying to get history re-written is beyond parody.”

And here’s a little roundup of the remaining Premier League reports from yesterday…

Elsewhere, Chelsea were held to a 2-2 draw by high-flying Hull City at Stamford Bridge.

Question of the day: when will Spurs score a goal? Tottenham fans, what do you think has been going wrong so far this season? Be sure to email in or leave a comment below the line.

Roberto De Zerbi says his Tottenham players continue to lack physical fitness and must “unblock” themselves in psychological terms after they drew their latest Premier League blank.

He explained: “There is a word in Italian – sbloccarsi – that literally translates as if we unblock ourselves.

“[It is] a mental block because four games, no wins, no goals scored … it is tough for the players. The team is extremely strong, we can score goals and we can win games. And then we have to respect the history of the players in their careers. Forget Dominic Solanke and Marmoush – the other players … they didn’t score many, many goals in their careers and we have to find these goals. I think we can do so with the quality of our play.”

De Zerbi added: “I said we started this season late for many, many reasons; too late. Many players at the World Cup, many injuries, many problems in Australia. Micky van de Ven suffered an injury in Australia. Domi Solanke the same. James Maddison the same. Mateus Fernandes suffered an injury in Australia. He lost 15 days and it’s not so quick. Sávio and Marmoush, they came 10 days ago. I started to work with this [whole] group not last Thursday but two Thursdays ago. So, I think we have not the right physical condition yet.”

Tottenham’s wait for a Premier League goal continues. It’s now 407 minutes and counting following a 0-0 draw with Everton…

Mikel Arteta was left furious with referee John Brooks last night, despite Arsenal’s 2-0 win against Sunderland.

Before Bruno Guimarães gave Arsenal the lead in a tight match that Régis Le Bris’s team were arguably unlucky to lose, David Raya made a brilliant save to deny Enzo Le Fée from the penalty spot. Arteta, however, did not believe that Ezri Konsa had hauled Dan Ballard to the ground, instead blaming the Sunderland man for pulling down his opponent.

He said: “We had to overcome a really tough opponent in a difficult place. Sunderland can suffocate you and they decided to be really physical and very direct and we also had to overcome a situation that, in my opinion was unacceptable at this level.

“I’m very worried and sad because this can never be a penalty. It’s a judo roll from the opponent. Ezri does nothing. We have to take responsibility to protect the game. Today the game was unprotected and it could have cost us the win and our momentum. I’m really sad. It should never have happened.”

Let’s take a quick look back at last night, when Arsenal earned a 2-0 win against Sunderland at the Stadium of Light thanks to goals from Bruno Guimarães and Bukayo Saka.

Hello, good morning and welcome to another Matchday live. We have two Premier League fixtures to look forward to this afternoon, including the small matter of City v United. Enzo Maresca’s new side make the short journey across the City of Manchester to Old Trafford, where they will go head-to-head with Michael Carrick’s men. The Sky Blues need a win to maintain their 100% record in the Prem this term and keep pace with Arsenal, who earned a 2-0 victory against Sunderland last night. Elsewhere, Coventry host Brighton as they look to get their first points on the board.

Over in Scotland, Rangers take on Celtic in a Scottish League Cup Old Firm derby at Ibrox.

We also have games in the WSL, Bundesliga, Ligue 1, Serie A, La Liga and Championship to look forward to.

“We can say that they scored goals, they won games. OK. But it’s completely fair to say that we didn’t compete before the start of the season with the same card. Maybe with the same rules, we could’ve signed some players that would have made the team better or scored more goals.”
Dave Estherby has messaged in about Tottenham and their (lack of) goalscoring. He says:

“Re. question of the day (8.44), yes, they will score (a) goal(s) - they will also finally achieve their, er, goal of getting relegated at the third time of asking. New manager, fortune spent, zero difference. Conte and Ange were right, it’s a business not a football club. As long as they can fill that stadium with Jay Z/Jacksonville Jaguars fans all is well.
“The fact Pochettino is now trying to get history re-written is beyond parody.”
And here’s a little roundup of the remaining Premier League reports from yesterday…
Elsewhere, Chelsea were held to a 2-2 draw by high-flying Hull City at Stamford Bridge.
Question of the day: when will Spurs score a goal? Tottenham fans, what do you think has been going wrong so far this season? Be sure to email in or leave a comment below the line.
Roberto De Zerbi says his Tottenham players continue to lack physical fitness and must “unblock” themselves in psychological terms after they drew their latest Premier League blank.
He explained: “There is a word in Italian – sbloccarsi – that literally translates as if we unblock ourselves.

“[It is] a mental block because four games, no wins, no goals scored … it is tough for the players. The team is extremely strong, we can score goals and we can win games. And then we have to respect the history of the players in their careers. Forget Dominic Solanke and Marmoush – the other players … they didn’t score many, many goals in their careers and we have to find these goals. I think we can do so with the quality of our play.”

De Zerbi added: “I said we started this season late for many, many reasons; too late. Many players at the World Cup, many injuries, many problems in Australia. Micky van de Ven suffered an injury in Australia. Domi Solanke the same. James Maddison the same. Mateus Fernandes suffered an injury in Australia. He lost 15 days and it’s not so quick. Sávio and Marmoush, they came 10 days ago. I started to work with this [whole] group not last Thursday but two Thursdays ago. So, I think we have not the right physical condition yet.”
Tottenham’s wait for a Premier League goal continues. It’s now 407 minutes and counting following a 0-0 draw with Everton…
Mikel Arteta was left furious with referee John Brooks last night, despite Arsenal’s 2-0 win against Sunderland.

Before Bruno Guimarães gave Arsenal the lead in a tight match that Régis Le Bris’s team were arguably unlucky to lose, David Raya made a brilliant save to deny Enzo Le Fée from the penalty spot. Arteta, however, did not believe that Ezri Konsa had hauled Dan Ballard to the ground, instead blaming the Sunderland man for pulling down his opponent.

He said: “We had to overcome a really tough opponent in a difficult place. Sunderland can suffocate you and they decided to be really physical and very direct and we also had to overcome a situation that, in my opinion was unacceptable at this level.

“I’m very worried and sad because this can never be a penalty. It’s a judo roll from the opponent. Ezri does nothing. We have to take responsibility to protect the game. Today the game was unprotected and it could have cost us the win and our momentum. I’m really sad. It should never have happened.”
Let’s take a quick look back at last night, when Arsenal earned a 2-0 win against Sunderland at the Stadium of Light thanks to goals from Bruno Guimarães and Bukayo Saka.

Hello, good morning and welcome to another Matchday live. We have two Premier League fixtures to look forward to this afternoon, including the small matter of City v United. Enzo Maresca’s new side make the short journey across the City of Manchester to Old Trafford, where they will go head-to-head with Michael Carrick’s men. The Sky Blues need a win to maintain their 100% record in the Prem this term and keep pace with Arsenal, who earned a 2-0 victory against Sunderland last night. Elsewhere, Coventry host Brighton as they look to get their first points on the board.
Over in Scotland, Rangers take on Celtic in a Scottish League Cup Old Firm derby at Ibrox.
We also have games in the WSL, Bundesliga, Ligue 1, Serie A, La Liga and Championship to look forward to.

articles.content:
The government apparently has an issue with paths for cyclists. Take it from someone who can’t ride a bike: this makes no sense

I ’m out of gas. Not metaphorically. Literally, my car has the barest minimum amount of fuel in it. This is not because I like to live dangerously , a la the great literary hero Austin Powers, but because gas is more expensive than ever. I have nowhere to be today, so I’m allowing my car to sit idle, empty and alone, lest my bank account disappear into the Phantom Zone of negative balance. If things get sticky, I can take public transit or, God forbid, ride a bike.

Except I can’t ride a bike, thanks to my parents, who were too busy doing more important tasks than teaching me, like arguing or falling asleep. But for many Americans, riding a bike is a perfectly normal thing to do. Am I humiliated that one of the many basic skills for life that I don’t know is considered so simple that it became a common idiom for something that’s easy ? Yes, of course. I don’t live dangerously, I live humiliatingly. Humiliation is my middle name. Dave Humiliation Schilling. Go on, point and laugh at the photo of me in this article. Get it out of your system so we can move along.

As I was saying, many people can ride a bike if they can’t drive a car for whatever reason, and they’ll be perfectly happy doing it. They smile broadly as the wind whips through the holes in their helmet and gently touches the exposed hairs on their head. They pedal like their lives depend on it (they do), dodging deadly automobiles operated by inattentive drivers. In some cities, there are dedicated lanes for these brave bikers, theoretically inoculating them from the dangers of cars pancaking them.

The United States has 4,400 directional miles of bike lanes , offering safety for anyone serious enough to risk it. The push for bike lanes began in the 1960s and grew in the ensuing decades. Theoretically, the lanes offer a carbon-neutral alternative to driving a car. If one chooses to bike instead of drive, it’s one fewer toxin-spewing death trap creating pollution and traffic congestion on the motorways. That sounds like a boon for the world, so naturally, the Trump administration wants to do away with it.

Condemning “ DEI bike lanes ”, the Trump administration has made a point of freezing or canceling related grants, referring to alternative transit options as unworkable in the United States, and suggesting removing the lanes that already exist. Their logic, if we are using that term loosely, is that bike lanes take space away from cars, create more traffic, and lead to chaotic roads.

I suppose that’s true, if we assume that there is an infinite number of cars and bikes are just extra, rather than an alternative that takes cars off the street. But that clashes with studies that say bike lanes actually make the roads safer by forcing drivers (sensible ones, at least) to slow down and avoid potential vehicular manslaughter charges.

Rhetorically, the administration’s charge of bike lanes being some form of diversity, equity, and inclusion makes no sense. If riding a bike is so easy, then how can we classify it as unique enough to be diverse? Children ride bikes. It’s far less exotic than, say, operating a motorcycle, which takes a special license in every state. Maybe if we had a dedicated lane for a penny-farthing , I’d buy this explanation. If I were tooling around on one of those, I’d never get where I was going, because scores of beautiful women would be stopping me every few feet.

Conservative disapproval for bike lanes stems from a blinkered, irrational view of culture, and more accurately, masculinity. Trumpists have teased Joe Biden and Pete Buttigieg for riding bikes. But I’ve been teased for not being able to ride a bike. Shouldn’t I be lauded for my commitment to machismo? My belief in the petrol-powered conveyance deserves commendation. My parents’ inattention to my development actually made me cooler, right?

If anything, I’m the diversity in this scenario. I can’t use a bike lane. I’ve been excluded from significant parts of the road. I can’t even walk in the bike lane. I should be furious, writing pointed, profane letters to my city councilperson, begging them to release me from my shackles. Or better yet, I should demand the city taxpayers pay for me to take bike lessons, so I can be accommodated. I’m the weirdo here. The one who has to explain my predicament, to feel excluded from the general population. Except, I’m not going to complain.

I might seethe when I have to swerve to avoid a biker. I might slam on my brakes when I try to turn right and a Schwinn comes screaming through the crosswalk. Maybe I complain for a living on the internet, but I’m also a responsible citizen of the world. I see the obvious benefits of bike access for those that choose to do it, for fitness or for affordability.

I can’t ride a bike now, but as my car becomes more and more of a money pit, voraciously hoovering up my meager income like the video game character Kirby , I see the benefits of learning, even if I’m in my 40s and will look absolutely ridiculous.

articles.title: Dining across the divide: ‘The young have so much idealism – but for him everything was determined by getting the Conservatives elected’
articles.summary: A Tory twentysomething and a lifelong leftwinger agreed on the need for more housing stock, but did they concur on welfare and net zero? • Want to meet someone from across the divide? Click here to find out how Oliver, 22, London Occupation Journalist for ConservativeHome Continue reading...
articles.content:
A Tory twentysomething and a lifelong leftwinger agreed on the need for more housing stock, but did they concur on welfare and net zero?

Want to meet someone from across the divide? Click here to find out how

Amuse bouche Oliver goes to a different park every Sunday to feed the ducks, and he posts where he’s going on Instagram. Others, usually his friends, join him, then they go for a pint

Voting record Labour or Green. In any general election under first-past-the-post, would vote Labour

Amuse bouche Adrian went coffee-picking in Nicaragua when he was 25 to show solidarity with the Sandinistas. He came away with an understanding of what was going on, and full of hope, which has since been cruelly quashed

Oliver He came in wearing shorts. I felt overdressed in chinos. But he was a really friendly guy. We shared a burrata watermelon chaat. Some coconut tofu. Hoisin duck pancakes.

Adrian It was all vegetarian, so it was mock duck. But I don’t know if he knew that.

Adrian As far as Oliver is concerned, it’s too easy and too attractive to claim benefits. I think the welfare budget has to be determined by the need that’s there. We shouldn’t do anything that stigmatises or penalises people who need support.

Oliver If the welfare bill keeps going up, no amount of tax is going to be enough. He said, obviously there’s people that need it. And I said, yeah of course, but particularly with young people, it’s been open to exploitation. The number of graduate claimants has gone up massively since Covid. We need to make it easier for businesses to employ people. Current legislation, employer national insurance rises, are making it harder.

Adrian You have all this idealism when you’re young, and I couldn’t quite work out what that was for Oliver. He seemed very politically minded, but in a very strategic, pragmatic way. Everything was determined by what might get the Conservative party elected. Without really any ideas or even an ideology, to be honest.

Oliver I’m a Tory. I believe in fiscal conservatism. The culture war, I don’t really care about that. I think people should be able to live freely.

Adrian We agreed we needed more housing stock. He thought we needed less regulation, whereas I thought there was a sticking point in terms of developers land-banking and choosing not to build houses, and wanting to build them in inappropriate areas, so you get out-of-town developments where people have to drive everywhere.

Oliver I said we needed to relax the planning system. I mentioned a specific niche recommendation: every window needs to be cleanable by 95% of elderly ladies. He said we need more regulation, the free market has failed. He thinks all new housing developments should have an inbuilt windfarm or energy source. I said that’s going to make it even harder to build houses. He thinks we need to be thinking of the future. I said we’ve got a shortage now – we should worry about the rest later.

Adrian There’s a clear case for accelerating change, cleaner energy, more electric vehicles, more heat pumps, a working home insulation programme. He challenged that in terms of who would pay for it, whether that would be passed on to consumers and whether people could afford that. My point was that you make polluters pay, to disincentivise pollution.

Oliver We’re both in favour of moving towards an economy that’s more supportive of net zero. We agree that there are job opportunities there. At the end of the day, net zero is an arbitrary target. There’s no real meaning in it. Kemi Badenoch doesn’t deny that climate change exists. She just wants to rethink how to tackle it in a practical way, rather than pursuing a policy blindly, without thinking about the possible consequences on jobs and the economy.

Adrian He’s clearly got the ambition, but maybe he will find a different way to channel it. I don’t know. It was a really nice evening and he’s a nice young man.

Oliver He was this really nice guy. By the end of the meal we agreed on quite a lot – we just want politics to be better and the country to be less divided. It was really wholesome.

articles.content:
Technology is going to drastically reshape the economy, and it’s within our power to decide what that looks like

T he idea that autonomous, thinking machines may one day destroy property, hierarchy and inequality is as old as western political thought. In Aristotle’s Politics, the philosopher cites a fantasy from the Iliad, in which machines begin to act independently of human direction, concluding: “If every tool could perform its own work when ordered, or by seeing what to do in advance … if thus shuttles wove and quills played harps of themselves, master-craftsmen would have no need of assistants and masters no need of slaves.”

The dream that automation could inaugurate a classless society is also present in the writings of Karl Marx. In 1858 he imagined the replacement of intellectual property with “socialised knowledge”, which would merge into a “general intellect”, blowing the foundations of capitalism sky high.

Today this prospect has begun to haunt Silicon Valley. In July, Dean Ball, head of strategic futures at OpenAI, claimed China’s advocacy of open-source models of artificial intelligence might bring about “full AI communism”.

For China, Ball complained, “AI is a public good which will ultimately be provided by the state as a kind of ‘digital public infrastructure’.” This, he concluded, “strikes me as a dystopian hellscape”.

Though I relish Ball’s discomfort, I doubt the rise of rival Chinese models – Kimi, Qwen and Deepseek – heralds the end of capitalism. Rather, it is an attempt to counter one strategy for global domination with another.

The US AI strategy – which is to hoard computing power, giving users access only via the internet – is designed to force the rest of us to use American software, cloud computing services and regulations. The Chinese counterplay is to make the AI open source, allowing users to run versions locally on their own servers and to firewall their data from being exploited by a Chinese AI provider.

Beijing gambles that if AI does indeed become a “general purpose technology”, the People’s Republic of China can win the battle for supremacy in the technologies built on top of it, such as brain-machine interfaces, bioengineering and what it calls the “low altitude economy” (the realm of delivery drones, and so on).

Who wins this contest will determine the trajectory of information technology for the rest of the century. But what if there was a third way? What if, instead of a contest between two flavours of hierarchical and unequal info-capitalism, we decided to shape artificial intelligence towards the ends Marx and Aristotle imagined?

Large language models (LLMs) already exhibit the features of what Marx described as the “general intellect”: they are designed to embody and learn from every item of human knowledge ever produced. Frontier models are already surpassing the output of some trained and experienced knowledge workers.

And while we are all aware that this has begun to eliminate tasks and even entire job functions, few of us have understood what it is likely to do to capitalism.

For now, of course, the monopoly positions carved out by the AI companies are making shareholders and the workforce very rich. But the job-destroying quality of AI makes it different from every previous technological revolution. Few can say with confidence that the jobs destroyed will be replaced by new kinds of activity – as vaudeville theatres were replaced by Hollywood, for example.

And it’s not just the jobs of workers that come under threat, but those of capitalists. If a machine can replace a junior solicitor, or a web designer, it can also replace the entrepreneur, the innovator and the forex dealer. The economist Philippe Aghion said that AI might not only automate entrepreneurial skill but destroy the link between innovation and profit: for who would patent a discovery if the filed blueprint could be immediately emulated and bettered by a machine? So we face a choice: delay and obstruct AI adoption in the name of social justice, or embrace it in a radically altered form. I prefer the latter.

Marx described the advance of industry in the 19th century as moving humans “to the side” of the production process, turning them into machine supervisors rather than machine operatives. Artificial intelligence does this for brain work, and to very high standards, less than five years into the deployment of LLMs. The impacts will be profound – because capitalism without human workers, innovators and entrepreneurs won’t function like capitalism.

So the rational question is not how Britain builds a sovereign AI to rival those of China and America. It is: how does humanity shape AI towards the fulfilment of human need?

There are some obvious starting points: break the link between work and wages, through the provision of universal basic services and incomes; promote co-operative and non-profit business models; and use AI to do what Soviet-style planning could never do – replace the market as the rational allocation mechanism. But that still leaves the question of what kind of artificial intelligence we need to design.

American AI looks like it does – brash, exploitative, secretive and mercantilist – because it is designed to replicate a specific social reality. Likewise, the Chinese models, for all their openness, are built to further the project of global hegemony.

It is not out of the question for those who want a green, social-democratic, co-operative or even anarchist future to devote resources in the here and now to diverting the path of technological development towards these goals.

If we are prepared to trail six months behind Claude or Kimi, we can simply use them to design an un-ownable AI model with humanism and universal values built in.

A green and social-democratic AI model would look very different even to the self-proclaimed ethical models offered by US vendors. It would aim to economise on energy and computing power; it might be weighted towards altruism, not competition and individualism. Its starting point might be the community, not the individual.

So while I don’t think AI automatically creates a classless society, it does stand a chance of creating a huge, generalised crisis of the existing model, in which those prepared to imagine the future, not cling to the past, have a chance to shape it.

Paul Mason is a broadcaster and author of Reds: A Global History of Communism (Apollo).

articles.title: This is how we do it: ‘Being in an open relationship means we’re constantly choosing each other’
articles.summary: Michael and Selena have three young kids and practise ethical non-monogamy which helps energise their relationship • How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously When you come back to your partner, you see the person you fell in love with Continue reading...
articles.content:
Michael and Selena have three young kids and practise ethical non-monogamy which helps energise their relationship

When you come back to your partner, you see the person you fell in love with

Selena mentioned wanting to have kids and be non‑monogamous on our third date – I thought she was being very forward, but I was open to both.

Our open marriage goes through different phases. We have three children under 10, and when Selena was pregnant and we were in the midst of raising babies there wasn’t much time or appetite for seeing other people.

Having children has the potential to accelerate the process that a lot of relationships go through, where things start to become all about logistics, as opposed to connecting as partners. When the babies were young, we fell into the trap of seeing each other as just another person you have to give care to, and that’s not sexy. But having a non-monogamous relationship gives you an opportunity to step away from that. When you are out with someone else, you’re just being yourself, and it helps balance out what can be a very demanding period of raising kids. When you come back to your partner, you see the person you fell in love with.

Neither of us has lots of partners. Typically we’ll find one or two people that we connect with, and then get to know them in the same way as if we were single – dating, which might evolve into a sexual relationship. Anyone we see always knows that our primary relationship and our family is the priority. That’s communicated upfront so there’s a clear understanding that I will always protect my relationship with Selena.

We manage it logistically like we’re going out with friends, coordinating and making sure that, for example, if one of us goes out on a Friday, the other will babysit and then go out on the Saturday.

Of course there’s jealousy and the feeling that I’m missing out. But ultimately that discomfort snaps you out of complacency. For us, that keeps our sex life and our connection alive. Plus, going out with someone else enables you to put your needs first, which then helps you to be a better parent and partner.

Dating other people was a way for me to come back to my own body after having kids

My relationship with Michael has been open since the beginning, 14 years ago, but we never did anything about it until our second child was two. After I had been birthing and breastfeeding what felt like continuously for four or five years, I needed to find myself sexually again. Sex had been tricky during that time because I was exhausted. Looking after babies, cleaning the house, cooking and then having sex with my husband felt like a pile of responsibilities. I felt as if I had no autonomy, which killed my desire.

Dating other people was like an electric shock. I still remember this feeling of having sex with someone in a hotel room for the first time. It wasn’t even that great – but walking out, I felt like: “I’m back.” It was a way for me as a woman to come back to my own body after having kids, which was so empowering. I’ve since found that it has played a huge part in awakening me as a sexual being. It has brought more intimacy into our marriage.

It was really difficult at the start, and it took many conversations, reading a lot about ethical non-monogamy and listening to podcasts. You have to write the constitution of your own sexual marriage, there is no script to follow. You have to work out every single detail. You have to be comfortable with feelings of jealousy. If Michael tells me he’s got two dates this month, I’m like, “Great, Netflix, ice-cream and quilting, that’s what I’ll be doing.”

Ultimately, being open gives an injection of fresh energy that you just can’t get after 14 years together and three children. It’s like Michael and I are constantly choosing each other. You’re going out there, having these potentially wonderful experiences with other people, and then you’re coming home and saying, “I love you. I love being married to you. I love having sex with you.”
