articles.title: ‘I’ve lost everything – my child, my house, my money’: how Israel’s war on Gaza has changed men
articles.summary: The impact of the conflict on Palestinian men is a largely undiscussed topic. Four civilians talk about their lives and relationships Before the war, Ahmed, 39, had a busy life. He was pursuing a PhD in factchecking and had three jobs: as a radio presenter, editor of a local factchecking website and researcher at an academic centre. He says he felt “happy” to be able to provide for his family while being intellectually stimulated. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The impact of the conflict on Palestinian men is a largely undiscussed topic. Four civilians talk about their lives and relationships

Before the war, Ahmed, 39, had a busy life. He was pursuing a PhD in factchecking and had three jobs: as a radio presenter, editor of a local factchecking website and researcher at an academic centre. He says he felt “happy” to be able to provide for his family while being intellectually stimulated.

But the war “blew our lives apart completely”, Ahmed says. Where previously he would spend hours lost in research, now he spends hours standing in line to fill water jugs or use the bathroom.

He says war changed his sense of self and that he no longer “feels the pillar of his family”, adding: “As a man, I derived my appreciation for myself from my accomplishments in my work and my studies.”

Ahmed had been living alongside his parents and siblings in the same building, each of his siblings with their family in a separate flat. In May 2024, they were all forced to evacuate their homes and have lived in tents ever since. He has found the lack of privacy in his new life hard and says it has created “emotional silence” between couples.

“Before, the home was a private kingdom, a place to decompress at the end of the day, to speak freely. Now life is communal and there’s no privacy. A man can’t express his emotions to his wife as he used to. Everyone can hear; they can’t discuss and work through issues as they used to.”

As a husband and father, he says he feels a responsibility to be a source of reassurance for his family. “I have children who don’t know what walls are, what a bed is, what stairs are.” He says he tries to make them feel that “everything will be OK”, but privately wonders what new hardships the war will bring and often lapses into silence. “That is the price of manhood in the catastrophe of this war.”

Back in 2023, Nidal, 40, says he ran a small business out of a storage room in his block of flats in Gaza City, selling mobile phones and home appliances on credit. He used to spend his days going from door to door collecting payments. “It wasn’t just work. I got to know people and had lots of friends and acquaintances. My life was good. We had everything we needed,” he says.

Both Nidal and his extended family, who lived in the same block, were soon displaced after an Israeli missile strike that killed his sister-in-law. In a further tragedy, his daughter Malek was killed after a second airstrike on a school where they were staying.

Nidal and the remaining members of his family eventually returned to the rubble of their home and erected a tent. The collapsed roof of the block of flats offers them some shade and shelter from the rain. But Nidal says he feels no hope of rebuilding his life properly again and spends most of his days by the tent, rarely speaking to anyone. “The war took away everything – my child, my house, my money.”

He says he feels a different person now, less calm and more angry. He feels embarrassed to ask his clients for money they owe him, given the loss everyone has suffered, and is sad most of the time.

“I can’t stand anyone and can’t even stand myself. I don’t even want to call myself an unemployed man – I am a man rendered helpless. Not helpless physically, but helpless in my ability to provide for my family. I secure for them the bare minimum that keeps them alive.

“May God spare every man from this: the breaking of a father before the eyes of his children.”

Before the war, Hussein, 24, had his own flat, was a technology student at university and ran workshops on AI. His life had a daily routine to it and he was thinking about finding a partner and getting married. Early on in the conflict, however, his home was bombed, injuring his father and leaving his sister-in-law in hospital for six months.

Hussein says he “started from zero … there was no food, no work, nothing”. To survive, he turned to whatever work he could find, beginning by charging and repairing phones before moving on to buying and selling them and providing technical support. He is proud that he managed to adapt and make money so soon after losing his family’s home, he says.

“I was very, very, very ashamed of myself at first. The war changed everything, even my future.”

He cannot imagine bringing a future wife into the tent where he now lives, “it’s not logical”, and says he must at least provide a home with privacy and running water. But he still hopes to marry and have children. “It [the war] has affected me and all young people. We have to repopulate this land and rebuild it. It’s us, the young people, who will fix it, restore it, make it even more beautiful than it was before.”

Hamza, 22, was a second-year medical student when the war began, spending most of his time at his desk at home in Jabaliya in the north of Gaza. But he soon found himself volunteering as an emergency frontline doctor after refusing to follow Israeli evacuation orders to move south.

There were countless patients with head injuries and only three neurosurgeons in the north. Working gave him purpose, he says. “It was an impossible mission for a student like me to work at the hospital and do the work I did. I consider myself a hero, to be honest.”

Hamza says war has changed his perspective on family and friends. He does not let his studying isolate him any more. “You always have to sacrifice something for something. The war changed all of that … and that is something I am grateful for.”

He says he has been drawn closer to his family. “We love each other more, respect each other more. We slept on the same mattress, sometimes in a space of two square metres. We were hungry together, we almost died together. We weren’t like this before the war. We became very tight-knit.”

Before the war, Hamza says he had put off thinking about marriage to focus on a plan to study neurosurgery overseas and be able to provide his future wife with a good life, a nice home and a car. But war and the death of family members has changed that, he says, and he now plans to start a family sooner.

“In war, when a person feels extinction, they are drawn to reproduce. God has made us this way. We have lost so much; there’s a feeling that we want to compensate.”

articles.title: Dramatic insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley
articles.summary: A recent spate of stark warnings about the dangers of AI has been met with scepticism by executives and investors.
articles.content:
Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs.

This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon.

Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity.

They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything".

Coxon is by no means the first AI insider to publicly sound the alarm. There have been a string of high-profile resignations from both Anthropic and OpenAI in recent years over apparent safety concerns, and some current Anthropic employees even echoed Coxon's post.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," a team lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, posted on X.

While Coxon said explicitly in his posts that his warnings were "not marketing", some executives and investors in Silicon Valley have reacted with scepticism to a recent flurry of insiders sounding the alarm.

Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings, and some in the tech sector have suggested the latest stark comments about the dangers of AI may be designed to generate hype by signalling the power of these products.

Anthropic's boss, Dario Amodei, has come under fire for saying AI technology could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and will "test who we are as a species".

One conference speaker, Grindr CEO George Arison, told the BBC he believed this week's comments from Coxon and others were indicative of an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic".

He called them "dangerous" and said they had prompted him to instruct some engineers at the LGBTQ+ dating app to stop using Anthropic's technology.

"It is irresponsible for us as stewards of our shareholders' money to be relying on a business that does what this company does, in terms of its public statements," he said.

"Maybe they actually believe it," Arison said. "Or you could argue they're saying it because it's a great way to gin up more investor support, because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"

Anthropic was valued at $965bn (£713bn) in its most recent fundraising round earlier this year.

In an essay posted early on Saturday , Amodei called for a slowing of AI model development and global regulation - and said the risks associated with AI were "serious".

Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'

Grindr CEO George Arison told the BBC he believed some of the stark public warnings about AI were "dangerous"

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang also discussed Coxon's comments before a crowd at the conference, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue.

Huang has previously said the notion that AI "is going to be the end of humanity" is "complete nonsense".

And while he may have a business interest in an AI boom - Nvidia builds chips that power AI systems - his comments reflect a growing backlash in Silicon Valley to the existential warnings from current and former staffers.

Some critics have even accused Anthropic of fearmongering in hopes that it will trigger a regulatory push that could shut out competition and leave it and OpenAI with a duopoly in the sector.

Brad Gerstner, who is the head of the investment firm Altimeter Capital, posted pictures of Huang from the conference and accused Coxon of "ridiculous hyperbole".

On Friday, the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, weighed in. Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it would acquire last week, was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year prompting an outcry over AI safety.

"Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," he wrote on X. "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."

Both Gerstner and Delangue were more circumspect on Saturday after Amodei's proposal was posted, with Gerstner calling the idea "an important step forward" in balancing competing considerations like speed and safety.

Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions proposed by Amodei.

In April, Anthropic roiled the AI world when it said it found that its Mythos tool could outperform humans at some hacking and cybersecurity tasks.

Mythos also showed the ability to independently escape what is known as the sandbox environment, setting off a debate among regulators, legislators and businesses about AI's potential dangers.

In a new development on Thursday, Anthropic said it had found and stopped threat actors who were trying to use its AI technology for activity including the development of bioweapons and cyber-espionage.

Beneath the sparkling chandeliers hanging in the stained-glass dome atrium of The Palace Hotel, some investors told the BBC that the comments from Coxon and others could accelerate a government crackdown.

Watch: "Slow it down" - Bernie Sanders proposes bill to ban AI superintelligence

Federal legislation co-sponsored this month by left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, known as the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, would impose a temporary pause in advanced AI development.

"There is a good chance that human beings will lose control over AI," Sanders told the BBC's Newsnight programme on Thursday. "And what happens then, nobody knows. But could it be catastrophic? Yes, it could."

"When scientists tell you there is a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he added.

If an industry-wide government crackdown comes, however, it is likely to be led by legislators and not the Trump administration which largely supports a policy of unfettered AI development. It has framed this as necessary to ensure the US does not cede dominance to China.

Speaking to reporters this week, President Donald Trump was asked if he had any concerns about AI leading to human extinction. "No, I don't have any," he said. "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now."

But the president's relationship with Anthropic has been turbulent. After the company refused to allow the US military to use its AI models, the White House described it as "a radical left, woke company" and designated it a supply chain risk, a move that a federal judge has ruled was illegal.

David Sacks, Trump's AI czar in the early days of his administration, has also levelled repeated attacks at Anthropic.

OpenAI has not endured the same level of scrutiny from the White House. When releasing a new model called Astra last week, OpenAI President Greg Brockman described his firm's relationship with the Trump administration as "a very good partnership".

At the conference in San Francisco this week, the pursuit of fortunes seemed to mostly trump any mounting existential concerns or fears over potential government restrictions on AI.

OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn, has previously announced plans to allow people to buy shares in its firm by listing on the stock market .

However, its chief executive Sam Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year, calling it an "ill-advised moment" to do so "given everything happening with safety" in an interview with Fortune magazine.

Meanwhile, one investor said he was looking forward to Anthropic's forthcoming S-1, a document a company must file with securities regulators in order to sell shares.

His main question about the company was simple: is the firm profitable?

When asked on Thursday if he fears the world may be coming to an end, Sid Sheth - CEO of the chip company d-Matrix which inked a deal with Nvidia at the conference that day - did not mince his words.

Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons

articles.title: ‘Really helpful’: the AI bootcamps aimed at addressing UK youth unemployment
articles.summary: Pilot project in Preston comes with apprenticeship offer for Neets at end of three-week course In a youth centre opposite Preston bus station , the UK government is trying to address two of the greatest challenges facing the national economy: AI and youth unemployment. The hope is that one will solve – rather than cause – the other. In a room at the recently opened Vault, a community hub in the Lancashire city, an “AI bootcamp” is under way – part of a trial in the north-west to give 16- to 24-year-olds AI training. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Pilot project in Preston comes with apprenticeship offer for Neets at end of three-week course

In a youth centre opposite Preston bus station , the UK government is trying to address two of the greatest challenges facing the national economy: AI and youth unemployment.

The hope is that one will solve – rather than cause – the other. In a room at the recently opened Vault, a community hub in the Lancashire city, an “AI bootcamp” is under way – part of a trial in the north-west to give 16- to 24-year-olds AI training.

The bootcamp tutor is standing in front of a video screen and guiding the five attenders sitting around a long table on laptops through a task designed to emphasise the importance of glitch-free data in AI models.

Everyone attending these sessions is either a 16- to 24-year-old not in education, employment or training – Neet, for short – or likely to join that bracket.

Youth unemployment is a problem in the UK. Nearly a million young people are Neet – just over one in 10 people in that age group. The advent of AI, either a threat or boon to the job market depending on your perspective, is now another factor to take into consideration when tackling the youth joblessness crisis.

Khudeija Rafique, who is attending the course, sees potential in the new tech. “It would be really helpful with whatever job I would like to go into,” the 18-year-old from Burnley says.

These taxpayer-funded bootcamps are a pilot scheme, open to 70 people who will undergo a three-week programme specially designed for Neets to learn how to build AI tools, understand how businesses use AI, and learn to use the technology responsibly. The retailer JD Sports, food company Heinz and IT firm Agilysys are among the partners offering AI apprenticeships specifically designed for the attenders to join at the end of the course.

There are two types of apprenticeship available: one for aspiring content creators to become AI marketing specialists, another to join IT helpdesks that need AI expertise. If a boot-camp trainee gets an apprenticeship, they will be going to an organisation that wants these skills and has an AI-focused role to fill.

“This is an opportunity to bridge a gap, to improve productivity and bring AI into organisations,” says Lauren Monks, an executive at IN4 Group, the company contracted to run the programme.

Amid general concerns about the availability of entry-level jobs and whether AI is stifling that market, being on top of the technology can be an advantage if you’re seeking your first job.

This is common advice from graduate recruiters, but experts say it can apply to Neets as well, depending on what sector of the economy they are joining.

Remy Simms, 17, is interested in applying for the content creator apprenticeship and says the Preston course has “changed my opinion” on AI. “It shows that you can work with AI and you don’t have to work against it,” he says. “I’ve got a better understanding of it and I know more about how it works.”

Alan Milburn, a former Labour cabinet minister, warned in a recent report that the country was “at risk of a lost generation” without government action on the Neet crisis. Milburn’s prescription goes a lot further than AI bootcamps – he calls for reform of the welfare system, for instance – and his report points out that work programmes by successive governments have failed to answer the problem.

Concerns about AI’s impact on employment have focused on the graduate job market so far, not on school leavers and non-graduates, amid expectations that it will be able to do the “grunt work” associated with junior employees in areas such as banking, consulting and law.

The impact on non-graduate work was unclear, according to Dr Bouke Klein Teeselink, who is researching AI and the future of work at King’s College London.

“We don’t have really good insights into how AI affects the non-graduate market compared to the graduate market,” he says, but suggests this scheme could help answer the puzzle of getting more young people into the labour market.

The key test of the bootcamps and ensuing apprenticeships, Teeselink says, would be the thoroughness of the AI training and whether these newcomers made a real difference to their employers’ productivity. “I hope the policy will be rolled out in a way that allows the government to answer both those questions,” he says.

So will the bootcamps make a difference to Neet numbers? Experts say there is no single cause of the crisis and any comprehensive solution must be multi-faceted.

Chris Goulden, the deputy chief executive of the Youth Futures Organisation, a non-profit that researches how to help young people find employment, says he does not believe AI is a driver of Neet numbers. The country still needs to increase the amount of apprenticeships it offers, and guide children who are not on a pathway to university into vocations, he says.

“Our sense is that AI is not driving the increase in Neets since the [Covid] pandemic,” he says. “It’s more to do with mental health issues and a general slowdown in the economy. But that’s not to be complacent, because AI is doing new things every day and it’s going to affect lots of jobs.”

Goulden says if the “first rung of the ladder” is being taken away by AI, it is logical to give young people a foothold in the technology. “Teaching young people to use AI is part of how we prepare them for the future,” he says.

Asked whether he wants the content creator or the IT helpdesk apprenticeship, 16-year-old Hamid Muhammad-Asif, from Blackburn, says: “I’m happy with both.”

articles.title: Residents and officials meet on dredging concerns
articles.summary: Officers plan to meet with a complainant in the coming days over the dredging at St Aubin's Bay.
articles.content:
Residents expressed concerns dredging at St Aubin could harm wildlife and be a danger to people

Harbour officials have agreed to meet with residents who are worried about sand and silt from dredging being left on a beach.

Letters from 24 people were sent to the Government of Jersey's environment department claiming dredging at St Aubin could harm wildlife and be a danger to people.

Minister for Environment Mary Le Hegarat said: "Officers will look to meet with a complainant in the coming days and review the situation before reporting back to me so of a course an action can be decided."

Captain William Sadler, Jersey Harbour Master, said he was looking forward to discussing the issues with locals and the environmental department.

Sadler said the dredging was routine, and helped maintain safe access to the harbour.

He added the work was carried out with the necessary licences and regulatory oversight.

"Ports of Jersey cares deeply about both the natural environment and the communities we serve," he added.

"We know how important St Aubin's Bay is to many islanders and are committed to balancing the safe operation of the harbour with protecting the character and environment of the bay."

In a letter sent to residents Sadler said the work was carried out on 19 March.

The letter added: "We note the concerns raised regarding seagrass, wildlife, beach conditions and access to St Aubin's Fort.

"While we are not currently aware of evidence linking the harbour clearance works to all of the issues described in your letter ... we recognise the concerns that have been raised and take them seriously."

The letter said that an in-person meeting would provide the chance to explain the background to the works and for residents to discuss their concerns in person.

articles.title: FastPasses, Mega Honey Deuces and $55 chopped cheese: welcome to the US Open in 2041 | Bryan Armen Graham

articles.content:
Craig Tiley says the US Open is going to become the ‘Disneyland of tennis’, and he means it aspirationally. Here’s what that might look like 15 years from now

T he year is 2041 and you’ve successfully made it through security and onto the grounds of the USTA Liquid Death National Tennis Center. Myla Rose and Leo Federer are hitting on Practice Court 23 ahead of their first-round match in the US Open Mixed Doubles sponsored by Botoxxify, the tournament’s official neuromodulator partner. Jake Paul, the 50th president of the United States, is a few hours from attending opening night with first lady Jutta Leerdam-Paul and labor secretary Dana White. Venus Williams has just accepted a wildcard into the women’s singles draw. You’re thisclose to paying off last year’s Honey Deuces on Klarna.

It’s been 15 years since Craig Tiley first used that shorthand before the 2026 US Open, barely a month after taking over as chief executive of the United States Tennis Association. Longtime Open-goers had already adopted it as gallows humor, muttering it between expletives on the outer courts during qualifying week, which for another few years was still free. That Tiley meant it aspirationally told you everything you needed to know about where New York’s annual late-summer orgy of sport, fashion and conspicuous consumption was headed.

Tiley’s grand vision was a future US Open with more entertainment, more extracurriculars and more “opportunities” for children and adults to experience things. At a tournament where the once-humble grounds pass already fetched hundreds of dollars on the resale market and chicken nuggets flecked with Petrossian caviar went for $100, the natural question was: more what?

We now know. Layers of access. Premium seating. Branded activations. An incremental, almost imperceptible erosion of value-for-money not seen in American life since the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 .

Prior to entry, guests are encouraged to download the US Open Experience app and select one of four admission tiers: Grounds Pass, Grounds Pass Plus, Grounds Pass Platinum and Grounds Pass Presented by FTX (they’re back now). Tennis is included with Platinum. Guests wishing to watch an actual match can purchase a FastPass to skip the regular queue for the escalator to the 300 level of Blackstone Court at Arthur Ashe Stadium. For an additional $85, the FastPass+ allows holders to briefly make eye contact with a player.

Fans in need of refreshment can relax at the Emirates Luxury Hydration Pavilion, where a bottle of water costs $31 but comes with a commemorative cap in the shape of a miniature Anna Wintour in sunglasses. Visit the Grey Goose Food Court for the Mega Honey Deuce, a 96-ounce vodka lemonade served in a souvenir fishbowl with six melon balls and one month of complimentary credit monitoring. Hungry? Viral foods are still mass produced as another layer of the fan experience. This year’s in-demand item is the $55 chopped cheese sandwich by Hajji’s Blue Sky Deli, now a Wonder property. (We’d suggest getting there early .) For healthier fare there’s an Erewhon located beneath Mamdani Grandstand in the space vacated by Lululemon after the company filed for bankruptcy during the Great Athleisure Correction of 2037. The merch stands nearby have been a Fanatics Experience™ for years now, so best to avoid machine-washing your $80 T-shirt.

Back in 2026, the USTA announced Kalshi as the tournament’s first Official Prediction Market Partner, hailing the deal as an opportunity to “pioneer that next generation of fan engagement while ensuring the integrity of our sport” while spamming push-notifications plugging the partnership to anyone with the app already installed. By then, spectators could already be found around the grounds staring into their phones and checking on their markets with matches unfolding a few feet in front of them.

Here in 2041, the concept has been fully integrated into the fan experience. Every seat in Ashe comes equipped with a small Bloomberg terminal offering live markets on the match, while the chair umpire pauses briefly between points so spectators can lock in their positions. Players are still prohibited from partnering with betting companies, naturally. Tennis has standards.

For those who prefer a more traditional gaming experience, there’s good news: a five-minute walk just down the boardwalk past the No 7 subway station sits the brick-and-mortar Hard Rock casino and sportsbook , erected by compliance-challenged billionaire hedge-fund manager and New York Mets owner Steve Cohen, where your eight-match parlay can still go up in flames the old-fashioned way.

The main draw starts on Saturday now. Once upon a time, the first round took place over two days: 64 matches a day, a delirious noon-to-midnight blur of tennis across the grounds. In 2025 it expanded to three days with a Sunday start, but the shrinkflation proved irresistible to organizers. Any sticker shock and belly-aching over ticket prices ended decades ago, not long after the nonprofit USTA handed over its ticketing operation to Ticketmaster to extract whatever the market would bear on its behalf. Few milling about the grounds today can remember life before dynamic pricing or digital layaway.

The scruffy democratic charms of the old US Open belonged to the same vanishing New York as Aqueduct and Jimmy’s Corner , but there are still traces if you know where to look. The bullring-like Court 17 is still the best experience on site when you can get in. A grounds-pass holder on Court 5 can still watch three matches at once. A late-night doubles match on an outer court, where the influencers are mercifully scarce, can still feel like the most important thing happening in town. Fans lucky enough to secure one of the tournament’s 400 remaining non-premium seats on Ashe, a dodgy experience in its best days , can still make out a tennis match happening down there from above the encroaching ranks of hospitality suites and Chase Sapphire lounges.

Some have called it enshittification. The industry jargon is premiumization. The trendlines in the USTA’s own publicly disclosed finances call it growth. Tournament director Morgan Riddle insists the changes are about meeting fans where they are.

Of course, even in 2041, there’s nothing cringier than hating from outside the club. The US Open was a victim of its own runaway success and its 2020s transformation into a playground for the affluent and blithely bougie was hardly unique in American life. Across the country – from Wrigley Field to the Rose Bowl to Belmont Park – ordinary seats were being replaced by clubs, suites and hospitality areas because corporations and wealthy spectators would pay multiples of what the displaced customers could afford. Can you blame the USTA for recognizing its showcase event had become one of the most coveted tickets in US sports? Who wouldn’t empty the coffers to watch 37-year-old Coco Gauff go for one last trophy and ride off into the sunset? There is enormous demand, enormous money to be made from it and highly compensated executives whose job – among the less glamorous responsibilities of a nonprofit tasked with getting more kids to pick up a racquet – is to maximize that revenue.

Maybe Tiley was right all those years ago. Maybe the proper response was to embrace the growth, build the suites, sell the experiences and accept that the US Open belongs as much to the people who come once a year for the ring-light Honey Deuce selfie as the rank-and-file diehards who once spent qualifying week scouting the up-and-comers on the outer courts for free. Those of us who preferred the old place had our time.

But enough with the remember when . Your FastPass window for Court 17 opens in six minutes.

articles.title: Spygate saga continues to haunt Southampton as case drags on
articles.summary: Manager Tonda Eckert’s future remains in the balance with the FA yet to decide over a suitable punishment Fifty seconds was all it took for the chant to begin. “You know what you are, you know what you are, cheating bastards, you know what you are,” bellowed the Bristol City fans, starting up a cry heard from every away contingent coming to St Mary’s Stadium this season. The Southampton supporters responded with sarcastic applause, then drowned out the noise with songs of their own. This is what life is now like for Southampton after May’s spying scandal – a saga whose full consequences are still unknown and could have ramifications for the season ahead. The English Football League acted swiftly after photographs emerged of a junior staff member hiding behind a tree to film a Middlesbrough training session, expelling Southampton from the Championship play-offs and deducting four points after the club admitted multiple spying offences, including on Oxford United and Ipswich. The Football Association’s case against Tonda Eckert, the manager, is taking far longer. And patience is wearing thin. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Manager Tonda Eckert’s future remains in the balance with the FA yet to decide over a suitable punishment

F ifty seconds was all it took for the chant to begin. “You know what you are, you know what you are, cheating bastards, you know what you are,” bellowed the Bristol City fans, starting up a cry heard from every away contingent coming to St Mary’s Stadium this season. The Southampton supporters responded with sarcastic applause, then drowned out the noise with songs of their own.

This is what life is now like for Southampton after May’s spying scandal – a saga whose full consequences are still unknown and could have ramifications for the season ahead. The English Football League acted swiftly after photographs emerged of a junior staff member hiding behind a tree to film a Middlesbrough training session, expelling Southampton from the Championship play-offs and deducting four points after the club admitted multiple spying offences, including on Oxford United and Ipswich. The Football Association’s case against Tonda Eckert, the manager, is taking far longer. And patience is wearing thin.

The incident left a deep stain on Southampton’s reputation, one that will take time to fade and will leave an indelible mark on their history. Fans initially felt a mixture of fury and embarrassment – their promotion hopes snatched away over smartphone footage of a rival’s training session. Still, it has not stopped them flocking to St Mary’s this season: attendances were a shade under 30,000 for visits from Stoke, Millwall and Swansea and a season-high of 30,132 made Saturday’s Bristol City match almost a sell-out.

“Initially I was disappointed and angry,” says Alex Watson, a 31-year-old Saints fan, outside the stadium before kick-off. “Then you go through all the stages up to acceptance.”

Frustration is now turning towards the FA for taking so long to confirm what punishment – if any – Eckert will face after being charged individually by the governing body. A fine or short ban would be manageable. But Bev Priestman was banned for a year by Fifa , while manager of Canada, after two staff members used a drone to spy on an opponent at the Paris Olympics, so there is precedent for a lengthy suspension. That would likely see Eckert be removed as manager.

It is nearly two months since the FA charged Eckert with misconduct , even though the EFL’s independent panel took a matter of days to determine Eckert authorised the spying and that it was a “contrived and determined plan from the top down” .

“The mood generally is the FA needs to make a decision,” Watson says. “They need to get on and do something about it, one way or the other.”

There is a lingering sense of inconsistency between sanctions for big clubs and the rest – an irritation shared across the country. Chelsea received fines and suspended transfer bans from the Premier League and FA for systemic breaches of agent rules between 2009 and 2022. Yet Southampton have been kicked out of a competition, docked four points and may lose their manager for filming some training sessions.

If anything, Southampton fans have begun leaning into the pantomime-villain role. On the hour, a chant of “We spy when we want, we spy when we want, we are Southampton, we spy when we want” broke out. Within a minute, Cyle Larin had put them two in front with his second of the match.

While awaiting a verdict, the club have been preparing for all eventualities. During a preseason friendly against Preussen Münster, Eckert watched from the stands while his assistant, Ben Garner, took charge in the dugout – practising how operations might work if the German is handed a touchline ban.

The scandal did not deter summer signings. The goalkeeper Daniel Peretz was a £6m coup from Bayern Munich, agreeing to make his loan permanent after playing through the storm. Larin made a similar commitment and the Canadian forward has scored eight goals in nine games. The fan favourite James Ward-Prowse, a star of their last Premier League spell, decided to return.

Early indications are that the team can be promotion challengers. Late goals from Kuryu Matsuki and Finn Azaz completed a thumping win. After the final whistle, Eckert walked around the Northam and the Itchen Stands applauding; the fans stood to applaud back. Eckert, who returned after the summer uncertain how fans would react, says their backing “means everything” to him.

Asked if he has found it easy to block out the looming FA decision, he said: “I wouldn’t call it easy. But life isn’t always easy, if you have big goals then you need to find a way.” He added: “The fans have every right to react differently to the situation, how it’s evolved over the last season. I would’ve respected every reaction and decision from the club, the board and the supporters. Either you can forgive or you can’t. That’s not my decision. It’s just to accept how the reaction is.”

Had Southampton not started the season with a four-point deduction, they would be level on points with the top of the table. Losing the manager behind it would be another cruel twist.

articles.title: The AfD won a shock election in Germany. Elon Musk was thrilled
articles.summary: The billionaire and the party have developed a symbiotic relationship to spread their far-right views both in Germany and the US The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party rattled European politics this week after a convincing victory in a German state election, which placed it only a few seats away from forming the country’s first state-level far right government since the second world war. Elon Musk was thrilled. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The billionaire and the party have developed a symbiotic relationship to spread their far-right views both in Germany and the US

T he Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party rattled European politics this week after a convincing victory in a German state election, which placed it only a few seats away from forming the country’s first state-level far right government since the second world war.

“Gut gemacht!” Musk posted on X a week ago, using the German phrase for “well done” as he congratulated AfD party leader, Alice Weidel. It was one of at least a dozen posts the Tesla and SpaceX CEO made about the AfD following the result.

The AfD reciprocated Musk’s praise, with the party’s Saxony-Anhalt leader, Ulrich Siegmund, thanking the tech mogul for his support. Siegmund, who wants German schools to focus less on responsibility for the second world war and whose top staffers include four former members of a banned neo-Nazi youth group , called Musk a “visionary”.

Musk has become a central figure in the global far-right in recent years, using his support and influence to back anti-immigrant activists, illiberal leaders and nativist parties. Along with a preoccupation with race in the UK , much of that attention has been focused on the AfD, and the major results in the Saxony-Anhalt election, and Musk’s jubilation at their win, have revived scrutiny of his connections to it.

Musk’s ties to the AfD and German far-right predate the Saxony-Anhalt vote and coincide with the billionaire’s own public rightward drift. His views on immigration, politics and race, which he expresses relentlessly on X, have over the years become indistinguishable from many AfD policies. In boosting the AfD and receiving their adulation in return, Musk and the party have developed a symbiotic relationship to spread their far-right views both in Germany and the US.

As Musk became more involved in politics in 2024, backing Donald Trump’s reelection with over $100m of his own money, he formed alliances with several other international far-right leaders who hold anti-immigration views and antipathy for democratic institutions.

Musk has appeared onstage with Argentina’s chainsaw-wielding Javier Milei, presented an award to Italy’s ultraconservative prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, then attacked Italian judges ruling on migrant rights and gave a livestreamed speech at UK anti-Islam activist Tommy Robinson’s rally where Musk claimed immigration was causing “the destruction of Britain”.

Musk also connected with Naomi Seibt, a German climate crisis skeptic and anti-immigration activist who frequently posts on X and was 24 years old at the time. Musk began personally messaging her after seeing her posts, Seibt told reporter Paul Ronzheimer of Axel Springer’s Global Reporters Network, and she promoted the AfD to him in their chats.

In late 2024, Musk wrote an opinion column for the German outlet Die Welt expressing his own support for the AfD. Musk’s op-ed claimed that Germany was on the brink of “economic and cultural collapse” that could only be solved by the AfD, which he called “the last spark of hope” for the country. He also argued that the party wasn’t extreme, giving the example that its leader Weidel has a same-sex partner who is from Sri Lanka.

As Musk took a prominent role in the second Trump administration at the beginning of 2025, he used his platform and newfound political power to further boost the AfD. In early January of that year, Musk hosted a livestream for Weidel that researchers found gave her a huge boost on the platform as well as translated to a jump in German-language media coverage.

“Musk did in fact have an agenda-setting effect on traditional media in Germany,” said Jan Rau, a researcher at Research Institute Social Cohesion and Leibniz-Institute for Media Research. “You could very clearly see it. There was a huge spike of attention from traditional media for Weidel in that moment, and a lot of this attention was actually connected with Musk.”

Weeks after hosting the livestream with Weidel, Musk also appeared via livestream at an AfD rally. Only days after causing an uproar for delivering fascist-style salutes at a Trump inauguration rally, Musk told the AfD crowd in Germany that there was “too much focus on past guilt, and we need to move beyond that”. His remarks drew condemnations from Jewish leaders and accusations that he was attempting to normalize the far-right.

Musk’s close proximity to Trump and prominent role in the White House following the 2024 election magnified his political power, as well as fears from foreign governments that he was interfering in their national affairs.

After acquiring Twitter in 2022, Musk made several changes that helped boost the divisive, far-right politics of parties like the AfD. He reinstated previously banned far-right accounts, such as pro-AfD, anti-immigration Austrian activist Martin Sellner – who has taken credit for mainstreaming nativist “remigration” policies – and often promoted international right wing accounts through reposts.

“The changes Musk made to the platform has made it much easier for far-right communication,” Rau said. “That’s helpful for the AfD in many ways.”

But researchers including Rau also argue that the rightwing bubble Musk has created on X has its limits. Only around 5% of Germans use X to find news, according to a 2026 Reuters Institute survey , and many mainstream figures in the country have publicly given up on using the platform. While some of Musk’s backing of the AfD crossed over to mainstream attention, much of it in recent months has been confined to his captive audience on X.

Today, Musk is deeply unpopular in Germany, with a YouGov poll last year finding that only 19% of the country had a favorable view of the multibillionaire. Fewer still, only 13%, viewed his attempts to influence German politics acceptable. Even within the AfD, Musk is not an entirely welcome presence.

“Musk’s boosting, in some quarters, is not particularly helpful,” said Oliver Marsh, an independent researcher formerly at the nonprofit Algorithm Watch. “A lot of the party are traditional German nationalists and don’t really approve of an American billionaire weighing in on German politics”.

While the AfD’s ascendance has more to do with Germany’s domestic politics and social dynamics than it does with Musk, it did not stop him from taking some credit for their success. Musk reposted a claim from a Germany rightwing media commentator that the tech billionaire’s ownership of X had caused a “vibe shift” that led to the AfD’s victory.

In the days after the AfD’s election success in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, Musk both celebrated the result and tried to claim that the party was not far-right at all but ideologically moderate. Musk posted that the party, which Germany’s own domestic intelligence agency last year labeled a rightwing extremist group , should be considered “far center”.

Musk also sought to reject American news media’s descriptions of the AfD being far-right, despite the party’s well-documented and extreme views on issues such as immigration, Islam and LGBTQ+ rights. Musk posted multiple replies to the Wall Street Journal and CBS News following the state election, attacking the outlets for using “far right” in their coverage.

“You are lying by calling AfD ‘far-right’,” Musk responded to a CBS News post on X , adding in another post that “‘far right’ is a propaganda term”.

The AfD party platform includes bans on public displays of Islamic beliefs; opposes same-sex marriage and adoption, despite Weidel’s long-term domestic partnership with a woman, which includes children; emphasizes ethnic-German identity and calls for mass deportations. AfD leaders also have received criticism over the years for downplaying the Holocaust and making provocative references to Nazism, with one of the party’s top members convicted in 2024 of using a Nazi paramilitary wing slogan during a rally.

Weidel has meanwhile claimed there is “a holy war against the German population” while calling for “remigration” , a term for mass expulsions once popular in far-right and white nationalist circles that has now been embraced by nativist parties as well as Musk and Donald Trump.

Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz responded to the AfD’s win this week by warning that the party’s true goals amounted to ethnic cleansing , a characterization which the far-right party denounced.

“If what is being advocated here, namely ‘remigration’, were to become reality, ⁠it would be nothing other than a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” Merz said.

Musk once again defended the AfD, reposting a user criticising Merz’s allegation to his more than 241m followers.

Musk’s views, which include a fixation on race and vocal opposition to immigration, have come to closely resemble those of Weidel and the AfD.

articles.title: Rise of the student commuters: weighing the costs of living at home or in halls

articles.content:
Changing social trends and creative timetables are making it more likely for students to stay at home while they study. Is campus life on the way out?

F or Lucy Brazier, a second-year business management student, commuting to university was an easy decision. She lives near Colchester, where the University of Essex is based. “[It] was the obvious choice for my course once I weighed up the costs,” she says.

And with overnight accommodation available on campus, she feels she gets the best of both worlds. “I can book a room at less than a day’s notice for £35 so I don’t have to drive home. I’ve used it after nights out, and the evening before exams so I don’t have the stress of driving in the morning. It’s been really helpful.”

Brazier is far from alone. More students are choosing to live at home while studying, and universities are increasingly adapting their courses and campuses to make commuting easier.

According to Ucas, 612,690 UK students aged 18 to 20 who applied before 14 January 2026 made at least one application stating that they intended to live at home – up 8% from last year’s figure of 569,880.

With commuter students now a significant presence on campus, Universities UK chief executive Vivienne Stern says the traditional model of student life is changing. “Universities are evolving to meet the needs of learners. Many offer flexible ways to access learning and resources, or adjust students’ timetables to suit those with longer commutes or other responsibilities.”

Amira Campbell, former president of the National Union of Students , says the trend has been building for more than a decade. In some cases, this is because students simply cannot afford the residential university experience any more. Many are students from non-traditional backgrounds accessing higher education for the first time, who prefer to stay close to home.

Universities have responded in practical ways. Manuel Souto-Otero, from the School of Education at the University of Bristol, says many institutions now timetable teaching on fewer days so students are not travelling in for a single lecture or seminar, while also reducing long gaps between classes. Extracurricular activities are increasingly scheduled in the afternoon rather than the evening and many administrative services have also moved online, reducing the need for students to make unnecessary trips to campus.

“Universities have improved transport to campus and parking options,” he adds. “They have changed campus spaces, in some cases opening new facilities close to bus and train stations where possible, and creating university buildings where students can work, socialise or rest between lectures.”

The University of Essex, for example, has introduced day rooms where commuter students can rest, store belongings and prepare hot food and drinks, as well as an off-peak gym membership designed around commuter travel patterns. At the University of Leeds, the commuter society organises events that finish before 8pm so students can still get home easily.

Changes like these also benefit students balancing study with work . If teaching is concentrated into two or three days, the remaining days can be used for paid employment.

Even so, commuting has its downsides. Time spent travelling quickly adds up, particularly where public transport is unreliable. “Around one in nine students spend more than six hours commuting each week,” says Souto-Otero. “Students who commute are also more likely than other students to say they received a lower grade than expected because they cut down on going to campus.”

George Charlton, 25, who studies economics at Manchester Metropolitan University, recognises the trade-off. “I was going into lectures thinking, ‘How quickly can I get on the train to get back?’”

Things have improved, he says, since the university introduced monthly commuter “chat and chill” sessions, helping students build a sense of community. It is also trialling post-lecture commuter sessions so students can stay on campus and avoid the rush-hour crush. “There’s definitely a demand for it,” he says.

There are plenty of compromise options, too. A degree is a three-year endeavour, and living in halls for the first year is a good way to establish connections early on, before moving back home. Another strategy is living farther away from the city centre in more affordable areas, or choosing a university where accommodation is cheaper.

For many students, though, university is still about leaving home altogether. It’s a chance to experience a different part of the country, meet new people and become more independent. “Not everyone is lucky enough to have their dream university on their doorstep,” says Campbell. “Moving away from home can open up more options for universities and courses.”

Gina Tindale, 22, is president of the Newcastle University students’ union. She says halls are designed with student life in mind and make it much easier to build that sense of community from the start. “There are gyms, cinema rooms, game rooms with pool tables. You can have a social experience and you don’t have to worry about train times.”

All this comes with financial challenges. Alongside maintenance loans and grants, many universities now offer hardship funds and bursaries to help with everyday living costs, while student unions provide support for activities outside the classroom. Student loans rarely cover the full cost of living, meaning parents remain an important source of financial support for many students, and paid work has become the norm for around two-thirds, so choosing a university with good local employment opportunities can make a real difference.

For those living in private accommodation, the Renters’ Rights Act means student tenancies in the private sector are becoming rolling agreements, allowing tenants to leave by giving two months’ notice. The change gives students greater flexibility if their circumstances change.

Financial considerations are only part of the picture. Moving away to study can also bring longer-term benefits, such as access to stronger academic departments, better internship opportunities and richer extracurricular experiences. According to recent research by Savanta, students travelling for 45 minutes or more were consistently more likely to report practical, academic and social challenges.

They were also more likely to miss out on the wider student experiences. “All of these are beneficial because they enhance your profile,” says Souto-Otero. “At a time when having a degree is not enough by itself, the quality of learning and additional experiences become important differentiating factors.”

Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institute, thinks students should look beyond the immediate costs and consider the bigger picture. “When all other things are equal, it is generally better to cast your net wide and consider the full social and educational benefits that come from living in halls with other students.”

articles.content:
As the final whistle blew Bruno Guimarães wore a mischievous smile, Enzo Le Fée was a study in dejection and Arsenal’s immaculate start to the season remained unblemished.

Two minutes after David Raya had rather majestically saved Le Fée’s second-half penalty, Guimarães delighted his new north London public and plenty of old friends in Newcastle by sending a shot curving past Robin Roefs from the edge of the area.

Mikel Arteta’s champions were en route to another win in a campaign that has now produced six victories in six games in all competitions, including the Community Shield. No one, though, should be deceived by the emphasis lent to the scoreline by Bukayo Saka’s stoppage-time penalty; this was most definitely the toughest test this term for Arsenal.

If Sunderland can keep playing like this, Régis Le Bris and his players should have real cause for optimism – even if they could have done without Reinildo’s late sending-off for felling Saka when conceding that penalty and collecting a second yellow card.

His penalty miss aside, chapeaux off to Le Fee, who has deservedly made Zinedine Zidane’s provisional France squad for the forthcoming Nations League matches. Sunderland’s attacking playmaker knew another good performance here could only enhance his chances of moving from longlist to shortlist and he did not take long to draw a foul and win a dangerous free-kick.

Arsenal’s former captain Granit Xhaka delighted in curling the meanest of dead balls in Dan Ballard’s direction but the home central defender, a one-time Gunners youth captain, could not quite connect.

There had been a similar reprieve for Le Bris’s rearguard when Saka failed to make the most of Declan Rice’s fine early delivery. Yet, bar a Gabriel Magalhães shot from distance that whizzed just wide of Roefs’s goal, a Kai Havertz shot on the turn saved smartly and a low 20-yard effort that Le Fée dragged fractionally wide of an upright, that was pretty much it in terms of first-half goalmouth action.

Mikel Arteta’s side were taking their time to establish a settled passing rhythm. If Sunderland’s superb organisation hardly assisted the visiting cause, Arsenal looked a little fazed whenever the outstanding Nordi Mukiele – surely another candidate for the France squad – advanced from right-back.

Ezri Konsa, meanwhile, did not appear to be either relishing or winning his extremely physical contest with Le Bris’s ever-combative centre-forward, Brian Brobbey. articles.content:
Georgia O’Keeffe inspires the latest Calvin Klein while Michael Kors feels indebted to Alexander Calder

C alvin Klein has taken a highbrow turn in the two years since Veronica Leoni took charge. The Italian designer, a philosophy graduate who was schooled in the chic design studios of Jil Sander and Celine, has shifted away from jeans, boxer shorts and logos, stripping the brand to its minimalist bones: slip dresses and simple coats, slim skirts and crisp T-shirts.

Leoni called this the “discipline of removal”. Her muse this season was Georgia O’Keeffe, an artist who the brand’s namesake founder admired. Klein bought O’Keeffe’s painting Summer Days in 1983 for $1m, subsequently donating it to the Whitney Museum. A checked pattern taken from O’Keeffe’s distinctive capsule wardrobe of utilitarian chic appeared on this catwalk as a wrap coat, hardware-free with a fabric belt and no buttons.

One nod to pop culture was allowed: a model in a crepe-back satin ivory slip dress, her blond hair scraped back by a simple headband, called to mind the late Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, the iconic Calvin Klein employee who was launched back into the fashion conversation by Ryan Murphy’s Love Story earlier this year.

Over at the Michael Kors show staged in the sunny courtyard of the Museum of Modern Art, the first model was wearing glossy black disc earrings the size of potato crisps suspended from glinting stainless steel hooks. They looked like pieces from Alexander Calder’s huge mobile, Lobster Trap and Fish Tail, which hangs in the stairwell of the museum.

No art heist had taken place, but Kors admitted to being indebted to Calder. This summer, the designer travelled with his husband to Paris, where a major Calder retrospective was held. “We were just in love! The magic of it,” Kors enthused at a preview before his show. Modernism became the theme for this latest collection.

As well as the Calder-adjacent earrings, there was an evening dress carved with crescent-shaped edges at the shoulders in homage to Matisse’s cut-outs, and a pencil skirt zigzagged with black and white stripes which winked to Carmen Herrera. A ribbon of banana yellow floating from the hem of a black dress was giving Ellsworth Kelly.

“I love the boldness of modernism and the optimism of it,” Kors said. After the bedazzled glamour of last season’s show, held in the Lincoln Center opera house, this collection leaned into a more artsy sensibility, with traditionally feminine colours swapped out for tobacco, black and moss green.

Held on the 25th anniversary of 9/11 , the show was also “a remembrance”, Kors said, and a tribute to the resilience of the city. “We keep going. Everyone said that no one would ever want to live downtown again,” he recalled. “And now look at us.”

Tory Burch has transformed her brand, once synonymous with logoed ballet flats and polished Upper East Side good taste, into one of the most directional names of New York fashion week .

Her show was accompanied by the eerie, unsettling soundtrack from The Shining, because “it’s quite dystopian for all of us right now”, she said backstage. The clothes were a cheerful contrast, opening with a lavender silk dress accessorised with a boa of golden silk feathers.

Jewel-toned pencil skirts, embellished cardigans and ballerina necklines had a midcentury sophistication. “I was thinking about how much people need to feel joy right now. We need to dream and escape, to find bright spots where we can, and that’s where this collection came from.”

articles.title: PlayStation gambles with 18-rated Wolverine game - will it pay off?
articles.summary: The BBC's Tom Gerken plays the hotly anticipated superhero game from Spider-Man makers Insomniac.
articles.content:
On Tuesday, Sony will release Marvel's Wolverine - the biggest game exclusive to the PlayStation 5 this year.

It's made by Insomniac, the studio responsible for the recent Spider-Man titles, which have sold 50 million copies in recent years.

But unlike the friendly neighbourhood superhero, Wolverine has a Pegi-18 rating in the UK, meaning a child cannot legally buy the game, and it contains considerable levels of blood, gore and violence.

It represents a gamble for the studio responsible for some of Sony's biggest hits - will it turn out to have been worth it?

This review does not reveal the game's biggest moments, but beware minor spoilers for some of the characters that appear and a few early sequences. Some of the images contain blood.

You play as Logan, aka Wolverine, the comic book superhero that can self-heal and has retractable claws.

Donning the famous yellow-and-black outfit (among others), you hack and slash your way through hordes of enemies.

The combat is free-flowing and easy to pick up, as Wolverine stabs and slices his foes with copious amounts of blood on display.

Combat is built around a "rage" meter which fills as you take down enemies, with a full meter turning your surroundings grey and allowing you to swiftly dispatch your foes

There are some stealth options, but I generally ignored them and went in with my claws out. The game didn't penalise me for this.

You also unlock a slew of abilities, much like other games in the genre, meaning you get even more powerful as the game rumbles on.

And a clever system allows you to spend the rage you have accumulated to regenerate your health.

The combat kept me hooked the whole way through the game, which took about 20 hours to get to the end credits. My colleague was faster, clocking in at about 15 hours.

You briefly mash the square button to regenerate your health after being beaten - meaning so long as you keep up your rage meter, you effectively can't lose

When Spider-Man released in 2018, it set a new standard for superhero games with an open-world New York City which you could freely (and entertainingly) explore by web-slinging through the skies.

It was so influential that it spawned a popular online gag, pointing fun at reviewers who couldn't help but repeat a cliché , external about the game making them feel like Spider-Man.

"There's a significant shake-up happening here in game design terms," freelance game critic Emma Kent told me.

"Insomniac is moving away from Spider-Man's open world formula to adopt a linear structure for Wolverine.

"That means less open exploration, and a more curated path through the game world."

The combat is broken up by short sequences where you explore high-detailed environments, which while fun at first began to drag as the game went on

It adds to the gamble that comes with the game having such graphic violence.

"Peter Parker and Miles Morales would go out of their way to avoid killing enemies - stringing them up or gluing them against walls with his webs - and there was no real gore to speak of," Kent said.

"Some games truly revel in showing detailed and over-exaggerated gore, but the violence in Marvel's Wolverine doesn't feel particularly gratuitous.

"When you build up a sense of flow, it really does feel like you're rampaging through dozens of enemies, and I think the blood splashes are an important way of displaying the carnage you're causing."

The reality is by having a higher age rating than Spider-Man, it is by definition reducing the amount of people who can buy the game. And the game's director Mike Daly accepted this came with a risk.

"Even though this character appeals to kids, making a game that is explicitly like, 'sorry, this is not for kids, you should not play this game' - it does reduce the scope," he said.

"But I think there was no other way to do it. That was the cost of doing business if we really wanted to set a game with this character in this universe."

The graphics are great, but small cutscenes like this broke up the action too frequently for my taste

Gameplay is frequently interrupted with cutscenes, which will I'm sure prove divisive.

Nonetheless, the acting is top drawer, with the standout being veteran performer Troy Baker (known for many roles including Joel in The Last of Us) who puts in a memorable performance as Nathaniel Essex.

Liam McIntyre, who plays Wolverine, told BBC Newsbeat he was "looking forward to people playing it".

"I'm so proud that people are resonating with the story, with the performances, the character," he said.

"I'm so happy that I've been able to make a Wolverine that hopefully people love."

And to that point - when Hugh Jackman's famous take on the character last appeared on the big screen in 2024's Deadpool & Wolverine, it made $205m (then £160m) on opening weekend in the US - the best ever opening for an R-rated film.

Deadpool & Wolverine ultimately grossed $1.3bn worldwide at the box office, suggesting there was a much bigger audience than expected for 18-rated violence

The way you leap from building to building is superb, and feels excellent to control.

But I'd rather there had been fewer acting sequences and more gameplay.

On one or two occasions, in a cutscene Wolverine did something which felt like it broke a cardinal rule of game design to me - never show the player something cool when you could have let them do it themselves.

"Troy and Liam in particular are performers where they get really invested in their characters and subject matter," Daly said.

"They are part of the problem solving squad for who they are and how they bring that out - they brought a lot to the table.

"They went above and beyond, and I think that's a big part of what made it so good."

Criminal Minds actress Nicole Pacent makes an excellent Mystique (right), while Spartacus lead Liam McIntyre is superb as Wolverine

I'll avoid discussing the story so as not to spoil it, but suffice to say I was engaged, even if at times I felt I was spending too long watching videos and not enough time using the controller.

Clearly the developers were inspired by narrative adventures like Uncharted for this kind of storytelling, and the gameplay even feels similar at times with chase and climbing sequences.

And while that game was genre-defining, it came out almost 20 years ago, so it's hardly a favourable comparison.

In fact, perhaps the biggest issue for Wolverine is that it doesn't reinvent the wheel like Spider-Man did.

It's a game packed with tight combat and excellent performances, but it never threatens to meet the genre-defining heights of Insomniac's previous offering.

And Daly said there was a "monumental" amount of pressure that came with making the game following the success of Spider-Man - but as to whether the gamble paid off, he took a Zen view.

"I measure success when I hear people talk to me about the game, who are Wolverine fans, and they say 'thank you for making this, you nailed it'," he said.

"If I hear that, it's like, yes, we did it. That's what we set out to do."

articles.content:
Toronto film festival: Erin Doherty plays a happily single mother in a downbeat town courted by an enigmatic James McAvoy in this expertly taut drama

E rin Doherty and James McAvoy both bring their A-game in this startling, involving movie from British writer-director Paul Andrew Williams, whose productivity and creativity continue to be an industry tonic. It’s an eerie mystery drama that Doherty and McAvoy perform with ferocious commitment. There’s something of Atom Egoyan or even M Night Shyamalan here … and I even found myself wondering if Williams intended us to think of Shakespeare’s Hamlet and Laertes’ lines about his father, Polonius: “… to his good friends thus wide I’ll ope my arms / And like the kind life-rend’ring pelican, / Repast them with my blood.”

We are in a downbeat British town, perhaps somewhere in the London estuary, a place to which a candy factory provides employment. Gina (played by Doherty) is a smart, capable single mum to 9-year-old Jamie (Smylie Bradwell); she works on the production line in cap and hairnet like all the others: much liked by everyone there. She is not fussed by the absence of Jamie’s dad and is perfectly content with hanging out with her friends and her sister (Liv Hill).

One night at a raucous pub quiz, for which she has had to hire a local girl as a babysitter to look after Jamie back at home, Gina finds herself drawn to an enigmatic, self-possessed guy standing by the bar, smiling benignly and drinking something non-alcoholic: this is Michael, played by McAvoy. With easy confidence and a quiet kind of authority, he chats to Gina and she can’t quite read this handsome man or read his intentions. Is he flirting or what? McAvoy’s Scottish accent also blurs the class distinction that may or may not exist between them. After walking her home, charming her and even love-bombing her with devastating compliments, Michael is the perfect gentleman and says he won’t come in. Later, Gina is even more fascinated to learn that Michael volunteers at a local food bank. But how does he earn a living?

Gina’s suspicious sister notes how well-spoken he is; she has perhaps picked up on something that the audience might also have noticed, that Michael has something secretive and supercilious about him. She wonders if he is or was a teacher, or if this food bank is some sort of court-ordered community service. But Gina won’t hear of any disparagement of this obviously remarkable man who is paying her the kind of attention she hasn’t had in a very long time. Michael comes round to their house and is a huge hit with Jamie; he asks Jamie if he likes computer games and goes upstairs with him to Jamie’s bedroom to play Super Mario Kart, while Gina, glowing at Michael’s quasi-paternal instincts, stays downstairs to chat with her sister.

Williams shrewdly controls the film’s growing, complex mood: a cocktail of dread, fascination and something else, as if Gina has been made a party to some occult conspiracy that Michael isn’t in any hurry to reveal. He already seems to know something about Gina’s babysitter that Gina herself hasn’t suspected. The film’s central dramatic events then kick the mood up into a higher gear. Gina is passionate, bewildered and Michael assumes the priestly air of someone who has seen it all before and who is either here to help or is some kind of vampiric outsider. The problem seemed initially to be that he was too good to be true. Clearly that isn’t the issue.

Williams’s alpha-grade cast present this tale of mystery with intelligence and focus and Williams shoots his principals often in looming closeup, as if the drama’s strange secret could be read in the faces themselves.

articles.content:
Toronto film festival: strong performances from two experienced scream queens and some surprisingly thoughtful direction can’t elevate yet another stalk-by-numbers horror

I t would be unwise and unfair to expect that Toronto’s genre-led Midnight Madness strand would open with quite the same jolt as it did last year with the record-breaking horror hit Obsession . That film was an outlier in almost every respect , both as it premiered and as it was unleashed on wider crowds, the highest-grossing festival acquisition of all time topping out at over $513m worldwide and sparking genuine Oscar buzz.

But it hasn’t curbed the thirst, or wider speculation, over whether anything might come even remotely close to what Curry Barker achieved and whether the festival might start to rival Sundance as the smartest place for new and exciting horror film-makers to premiere their debut projects. The jury is out with the festival having just begun, but the Midnight strand is off to a far less notable start this time around with the mostly unremarkable survival slasher River, a film directed with flashes of artfulness but written with an overwhelm of familiarity. Writer-director debuts have increasingly tended to follow that pattern (it’s OK not to do everything!) and I think Joshua Giuliano has at least shown enough visual potential here to ably steer someone else’s script to screen next time.

It’s a shame as I do have a soft spot for the rare horror films that centre siblings over romantic pairings or friends, adding a different kind of emotional texture and more intense dramatic stakes to films like Ginger Snaps, House of Wax and, especially, Jeepers Creepers. In River it’s two sisters and a brother, all coming together to scatter their father’s ashes on the, you guessed it, river where he spent most of his days. A more bonded younger sister and brother (Jane Levy and Max Mattern) are still living at the family home and they are joined by their somewhat estranged older sister (Jessica Rothe) who has less fond memories of their late dad. There’s the expected tension before they even get on the boat and through a convoluted set of circumstances, the trio find themselves stranded in the middle of the river. Bad enough without a bloodied guy in a skin mask standing on the bank.

Giuliano starts with a surprisingly artful cold open that expands upon a nifty idea he had for a 2019 short film , which shows us the bloodied aftermath of an abandoned car and plays the sound of what led up to that scene. It’s incredibly effective and, for the genre, incredibly unusual although it does suggest that we might be heading somewhere equally as inventive and as the film unfolds, we find ourselves drifting backward rather than forward. It’s not that River needed to reinvent a very rusty wheel but even when going through the motions, Giuliano can’t quite find the right pacing or energy level to get us inching toward the edge of our seats. It’s just never scary or propulsive enough and despite the tease of some character development at the start, itself a rarity in a slasher, there’s not enough specificity or spark to the sibling dynamic to have us willing them to survive.

It’s comfortable territory for both Levy and Rothe, though, the former enduring all kinds of hell in both Don’t Breathe and 2013’s Evil Dead and the latter being the very best part of the one-trick Happy Death Day series, each deserving of contemporary scream queen status. They make the most of the least, adding edge to often edgeless dialogue, and perhaps some hardcore fans will enjoy them both causing maximum damage in an elongated climax that goes full-on with the body-puncturing, eye-popping, head-removing gore. But Giuliano can’t find them a worthy antagonist because while shirtless 6ft 8in basketball player turned Predator monster Dane DiLiegro certainly has an imposing look (even if he often looks more like he’s going to a Fire Island Halloween party), the film isn’t sure how much or how little we should know about his motivations and backstory. Giuliano opts for the frustrating sour spot in between not enough and too much and none of it is as skin-crawlingly creepy as he seems to think it is. A final mid-credits scene, which brings back the sound device and sets up a cinematic universe we could easily do without, suggests that Giuliano is sure that his River will lead into an ocean. I think he might have already run dry.

River is premiering at the Toronto film festival and will be out in cinemas and available on Shudder in 2027
